articles.title: Fed Minutes Show Another Rate Hike Is Likely This Year as Kevin Warsh's FOMC Battles Persistent Inflation. Here's Why That Signal Matters for Stocks and Bonds Heading Into Year-End. - The Motley Fool
articles.summary: Fed Minutes Show Another Rate Hike Is Likely This Year as Kevin Warsh's FOMC Battles Persistent Inflation. Here's Why That Signal Matters for Stocks and Bonds Heading Into Year-End.  The Motley Fool
articles.full_text:
According to the latest meeting minutes released Oct. 7 by the Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), Kevin Warsh and the other central bankers are planning to hike interest rates again in 2026. The FOMC has two more meetings left this year, Oct. 28 and Dec. 9, to decide on possible Fed rate hikes by year-end.
Inflation seems to be sticking around like an unwanted houseguest. The most recent CPI report showed that consumer prices rose 3.7% year over year in September 2026. After raising interest rates in September, it looks like the Fed is going to have to hike by another quarter percentage point or possibly half percentage point by the end of this year.
Let's look at a few high-level impacts of Fed interest rate hikes and what they mean for investors in stocks and bonds.
Higher interest rates: Bad for stocks (usually)
When the Fed hikes interest rates, it's trying to reduce the money supply and slow down the economy. It's trying to make money more expensive, make borrowing more expensive, and hopefully reduce inflation. When there are too many dollars chasing too few goods and services, that drives inflation higher. When there are fewer dollars in the economy, that tends to drive down inflation.
But cutting inflation, while necessary, can be bad in the short run for stock prices. Higher interest rates mean higher borrowing costs. Loans and consumer credit get more expensive. Lots of people might decide not to buy a new car this year, not to apply for a home mortgage, not to open a new credit card. Business leaders make decisions based on higher interest rates, too. Higher costs of business borrowing might make companies decide not to build a new factory, not to hire new employees, not to invest in future growth.
All of this can be bad for stocks. In 2022, the last time the Fed was hiking interest rates aggressively, the S&P 500 index (^GSPC +0.28%) declined by about 19%, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 was down about 33%.
We might not be on the verge of that same kind of 2022-style rate-driven stock market crash. Kevin Warsh and the Fed seem to be making smaller adjustments. Stock market investors should be cautious, but not panicking right now. If you're a long-term investor, buying a low-cost index fund like the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO +0.31%) could still be a great choice.
Recent research from Vanguard suggests that Fed rate hikes won't hurt the stock market in the short run -- rates might need to go at least a percentage point higher before the stock market would suffer negative effects. There's never a 100% "safe" time to buy stocks, but a few Fed rate hikes right now don't seem like a big enough reason to be bearish.
Higher interest rates: Better for bonds? (maybe)
Warsh and the Fed's FOMC don't control all interest rates -- only the short-term effective federal funds rate. But when the Fed hikes interest rates, longer-term bond yields tend to go higher, too. And when bond yields go up, bond prices go down. Higher rates and lower bond prices can be a sign for investors to "buy the dip" on bonds.
Buying bonds at today's higher rates and lower prices can become a better deal for bond investors. When risk-free U.S. government bond yields are at 5% or higher, that might make many investors stop and think, "Maybe I'd like to buy bonds instead of stocks, and lock in that safe yield."
If you want to buy bonds at today's higher interest rates, the Vanguard Total Bond Market ETF (BND +0.21%) is a simple, low-cost way to put thousands of high-quality U.S. bonds in your portfolio.

articles.title: Bank of America Expects Fed Rate Hike in October Despite 20% Market Odds - News and Statistics - IndexBox
articles.summary: Bank of America Expects Fed Rate Hike in October Despite 20% Market Odds - News and Statistics  IndexBox
articles.full_text:
Bank of America Maintains October Fed Rate Hike Forecast Ahead of October 28 Decision
Bank of America analysts reiterated their expectation that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates in October, according to Investing.com. The bank made the case in a note issued Monday, ahead of the central bank's next rate decision, which is scheduled for Wednesday, October 28.
Market pricing currently assigns a 20% probability to a rate increase at that meeting, the bank noted. Bank of America nonetheless maintained its forecast, citing September inflation data as strengthening the argument for an October move.
The bank observed that the inflation picture has deteriorated since the September meeting. It also projected that core PCE could plausibly finish the year at 3.4% year over year, pointing to the risk that an energy shock gets passed through amid a booming nominal economy.
Bank of America highlighted that most of the Federal Open Market Committee supported two rate hikes this year. On that basis, it questioned why the committee would forgo the second increase in October while preserving the option for a third in December.
The bank concluded that the decision ultimately depends on the character of Chair Walsh. It described its conviction as low regarding whether he is serious about bringing a sea change to the Fed, but said it was giving him the benefit of the doubt by retaining its October hike forecast.

articles.title: GBP/USD Forecast: Strong UK Jobs Data Lifts Pound Serling, BoE Rate Hike Bets - CurrencyNews.co.uk
articles.summary: GBP/USD Forecast: Strong UK Jobs Data Lifts Pound Serling, BoE Rate Hike Bets  CurrencyNews.co.uk
articles.full_text:
The Pound to US Dollar (GBP/USD) exchange rate moved higher on Tuesday after unexpectedly strong UK employment figures reinforced expectations that the Bank of England (BoE) will raise interest rates in November.
At the time of writing, GBP/USD was trading at around $1.3346, up approximately 0.3% from Tuesday's opening levels.
Sterling found fresh support after the latest UK labour market report delivered a considerably stronger performance than economists had anticipated.
Figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) showed the unemployment rate fell from 4.9% to 4.7% in the three months to August, defying expectations for a broadly unchanged reading.
Employment also increased by 102,000, comfortably exceeding forecasts for a rise of just 20,000.
Wage growth provided further encouragement for Pound investors.
Regular earnings, excluding bonuses, accelerated from 3.6% to 3.7% year-on-year, suggesting that underlying pay pressures remain persistent despite earlier signs of a cooling labour market.

The stronger figures reinforced expectations that the BoE will deliver another 25-basis-point interest rate increase at its November meeting.
With unemployment falling and wage growth remaining firm, policymakers may have less reason to delay further tightening, particularly while inflation continues to exceed the Bank's 2% target.
The prospect of higher UK borrowing costs helped Sterling strengthen against several of its major counterparts.
The US Dollar (USD), meanwhile, struggled to attract demand on Tuesday as improving market sentiment reduced appetite for traditional safe-haven currencies.
Although oil prices remained elevated and concerns persisted over the possibility of renewed escalation in the Middle East, investors showed a greater willingness to hold riskier assets.
Expectations that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates more gradually than previously anticipated also limited support for the 'Greenback'.
US political developments added another source of uncertainty.
Recent polling suggesting stronger support for the Democrats ahead of the mid-term elections raised questions over whether President Donald Trump could face greater opposition to his legislative agenda.
However, the Dollar's losses remained relatively contained as investors continued to monitor geopolitical risks and the outlook for US monetary policy.
Near-Term GBP/USD Forecast: UK Inflation Could Extend Sterling's Gains
Wednesday's UK consumer price index (CPI) release will provide the next major test for the Pound to US Dollar exchange rate.
Economists expect annual headline inflation to accelerate from 3.1% to 3.4% in September, adding to concerns that price pressures remain stubbornly elevated.
Following Tuesday's stronger employment figures, an above-forecast inflation reading would strengthen the case for another Bank of England rate increase in November.
This could allow Sterling to build on its latest gains and challenge the $1.3400 level.
However, a softer inflation reading could temper expectations for further tightening and encourage some profit-taking following the Pound's recent recovery.
For the US Dollar, the absence of major economic releases may leave broader market sentiment as the main influence on trading.
Renewed geopolitical tensions or a deterioration in risk appetite could revive demand for the safe-haven Dollar, potentially limiting GBP/USD's upside.

articles.title: EUR/USD Price Forecast: Euro at 1.1215 as French OAT Spread Hits 152.5 bps Before Fed-ECB Week — 1.1150 Target - TradingNEWS
articles.summary: EUR/USD Price Forecast: Euro at 1.1215 as French OAT Spread Hits 152.5 bps Before Fed-ECB Week — 1.1150 Target  TradingNEWS
articles.full_text:
Key Points
- The French OAT-Bund spread widened 5.5 bps to 152.5 bps as 10-year OAT yields rose to 4.96%.
- EUR/USD has failed four times at the 1.1260–1.1270 resistance zone since early October.
- Euro area inflation jumped to 3.8% in September, keeping an ECB hike in play for October 29.
EUR/USD traded at 1.1215 in New York on Tuesday, down 0.22% from Monday’s 1.1239 close, after a session that ran from a low of 1.1182 to a high of 1.1235. The European Central Bank fixed its reference rate at 1.1215, down from 1.1225 on Monday and 1.1253 last Friday. The euro opened the European morning at 1.1212, rallied to 1.1235 as the dollar softened on fading October Fed hike bets, then gave the entire move back when Brent crude spiked above $111. The pair has spent October inside a 156-pip band between 1.1114 and 1.1270.
The thesis for this forecast is simple. The euro is carrying a French fiscal risk premium and a rate disadvantage against the dollar, and neither will shift until the Federal Reserve decides on October 28 and the ECB decides on October 29. French 10-year yields rose 3 basis points to 4.96% on Tuesday, and the OAT-Bund spread widened 5.5 basis points to 152.5 basis points. The Fed funds target sits at 3.75% to 4.00% against an ECB deposit rate of 2.50%. Euro area inflation jumped to 3.8% in September, which gives the ECB a reason to hike, but French political unrest gives it a reason to hold.
The longer picture is a steady grind lower. EUR/USD is down 3.78% over the past year and 2.19% over the past month. It traded at 1.2079 at its 52-week high and averaged 1.1588 for 2026 so far, against 1.1276 in 2025. The six-month high was 1.1786 on May 9. At 1.1215, the euro trades 7.2% below its 52-week high and just 0.9% above the October 14 low of 1.1114, its lowest level in 17 months.
The euro failed to join the rally that lifted most major currencies against the dollar on Tuesday morning. GBP/USD firmed to 1.3348 after a stronger-than-expected UK jobs report, and the yen gained as authorities watched for excessive moves. The euro lagged both. A currency that cannot rise on a weaker dollar is carrying its own problem, and in this case the problem is France.
The calendar sets the timing. The Fed decides on October 28, and the ECB decides the following day at 14:15 CET, with President Christine Lagarde’s press conference at 14:45 CET. For the first time this cycle, the ECB will vote knowing whether the rate gap with the United States has just widened again.
OAT Yields at 4.96%, Spread at 152.5 bps: The French Risk Premium
French government debt is the single largest weight on the euro. The 10-year OAT yield rose 3 basis points to 4.96% on Tuesday, after its biggest daily rise in nearly a month on Monday. The yield reached 4.9937% in early October, its highest level since July 2002. The spread over German Bunds widened 5.5 basis points to 152.5 basis points on Tuesday. It hit 158.67 basis points in early October, the widest since November 2011, at the height of the euro zone sovereign debt crisis.
The pace of the widening is what alarms currency traders. The OAT-Bund spread broke above 100 basis points in September for the first time since 2012. By October 1, it was above 130 basis points. By early October it had reached 158.67. A move of almost 60 basis points in a month is a pace matched only during the euro crisis. On Monday, the spread stood at 142.3 basis points, with the OAT at 4.85% against 3.43% for the Bund. Tuesday’s jump to 152.5 basis points erased most of the recent stabilization.
The political trigger is visible on the streets. Protest groups announced a new round of demonstrations for Saturday, and recent street violence included the burning of Limoges city hall. The National Assembly votes on the budget on October 20 and October 27, which puts two fiscal decision points inside the same window as the Fed and ECB meetings. Long-term investors have stepped back ahead of the vote, and market depth in French debt has fallen to less than half its normal level.
The broader bond move adds to the pressure. Since the start of the Hormuz crisis, 10-year OAT yields have risen 150 basis points, against 115 basis points for U.S. Treasuries. France is the hardest hit in the global bond sell-off, mostly because of its own fiscal and political problems. Realized volatility in the OAT spread has jumped to the 90th percentile.
The currency channel is direct. When foreign investors sell French bonds, they sell euros. When the spread widens, it signals that investors see rising fiscal and political risk in France relative to Germany, and that risk feeds into the single currency. A spread of 150 basis points is widely treated as a tipping point. Above it, the risk of contagion into Italian and Spanish debt rises, along with the pressure on the ECB to respond.
The euro’s weakness this month maps closely onto the spread. EUR/USD hit its October low of 1.1114 as the spread approached its peak and recovered to 1.1269 last Friday as it narrowed. Tuesday’s widening to 152.5 basis points coincided with the euro’s slide back to 1.1182.
ECB Deposit Rate 2.50% vs Fed Funds 3.75% to 4.00%
The second weight on the euro is the policy gap. The ECB deposit rate stands at 2.50%, where it has been since September 16, after a quarter-point hike on September 10. The main refinancing rate sits at 2.65% and the marginal lending rate at 2.90%. The Fed funds target range stands at 3.75% to 4.00%. The gap between the two policy rates is between 125 and 150 basis points, and it favors the dollar.
The ECB has been tightening, but slowly. It raised rates in June for the first time since 2023, taking the deposit rate to 2.25%, and became the first major central bank to hike in response to the Middle East war. The September move took it to 2.50%. Lagarde has stressed that the bank is not pre-committing to a path and will decide meeting by meeting. She has also said she sees no signs of second-round inflation effects yet.
The Fed has been tightening faster. The September hike was its first in three years. Futures now price an 82% chance of a hold at the October 27 and 28 meeting and an 89% chance of a hike in December. If the Fed hikes in December and the ECB does not, the gap widens to between 150 and 175 basis points.
Bond yields tell the same story at longer maturities. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield traded at 5.10% on Tuesday. The German 10-year Bund yielded 3.43% on Monday and edged lower on Tuesday. That leaves a U.S.-German 10-year spread of 167 basis points. Every basis point of that spread is a reason for global investors to hold dollars rather than euros.
Forward pricing reflects the carry. The one-week forward rate for EUR/USD stands at 1.1242, the one-month at 1.1255, the three-month at 1.1284, the six-month at 1.1327 and the one-year at 1.1416. Those forward rates sit above spot because U.S. rates are higher than euro rates. They measure the interest-rate differential, not an expectation that the euro will rise.
Lagarde has added a twist to the policy debate. She said long-term interest rates have climbed since the September meeting, which will slow growth and reduce the pass-through of energy costs by more than the ECB projected. In effect, she counted the bond market selloff as part of the tightening. Currency traders read that as a signal of fewer ECB hikes, and therefore a smaller rate lift for the euro against a dollar backed by the Fed’s higher policy rate.
Euro Area Inflation Hit 3.8% in September, the Highest in Two Years
Inflation is the reason the ECB cannot step back, and it is the strongest argument for the euro bulls. Euro area annual inflation accelerated to 3.8% in September from 3.2% in August, above the 3.6% forecast. That reading is the highest in the past 24 months. Monthly inflation ran at 0.6%, up from 0.4% in August. Core inflation, which excludes energy and food, rose to 2.5% from 2.4%, in line with expectations.
Energy is driving the headline. Energy inflation in the euro area reached 18.8% in September, up from 14.3% in August. The euro area imports most of its oil and gas, so Brent at $106 to $111 hits European consumers and businesses harder than American ones. Germany’s annual inflation rose to 3.3% from 2.9%, its highest in two years. Austria hit 3.5% and Greece 5.1%.
The ECB’s own forecasts show how persistent the problem is. The bank kept its 2026 inflation forecast at 3.0% but revised its projections higher for 2027 and 2028, to 2.5% and 2.1%. Consumer inflation expectations stood at 3.0% in August, and three-year expectations rose to 2.9%. With headline inflation nearly twice the 2% target, the bank has little room to stop hiking.
The core figure is the one that matters for the October 29 decision. Core inflation is closer to the second-round effects Lagarde has said the ECB has not seen yet. A core reading of 2.5% sits at the edge of that line. If core accelerates further, the measured approach to hiking will be tested.
Inflation helps the euro only if it forces the ECB to tighten faster than the Fed. That is the bull case: a hawkish ECB surprise on October 29, paired with a Fed that holds on October 28, would narrow the rate gap and lift the euro. Markets do not price that scenario. Expectations for further ECB tightening point to December rather than October, with an October move possible but unlikely. Earlier in the cycle, the market priced only an 11.7% probability of an October hike.
The risk for the euro is that inflation stays high while growth weakens. Energy at 18.8% eats into household spending, and higher bond yields raise borrowing costs for governments and companies. That combination of high inflation and slowing growth is the stagflation scenario, and it is negative for any currency because it forces the central bank to choose between fighting prices and supporting the economy.

articles.title: Gold market consolidating rather than entering bear market, Metals Focus analyst says - TradingView
articles.summary: Gold market consolidating rather than entering bear market, Metals Focus analyst says  TradingView
articles.full_text:
Gold's inability to sustain a rally since its correction earlier this year reflects competition for investment capital rather than a fundamental deterioration in the metal's long-term outlook, Metals Focus director of gold and silver Matthew Piggott said Monday in an interview with Kitco.com.
Piggott said institutional investors have consistently returned to the gold market when prices have fallen toward $4,000/oz, "so we've had kind of a floor established, and central banks have been a big part of that too."
The underlying economic and geopolitical factors that supported gold's rally in 2025 have not disappeared; if anything, growing government debt and fiscal uncertainty have strengthened gold's longer-term investment case, Piggott said.
Large government deficits, rising debt-servicing costs, and uncertainty surrounding U.S. policy should continue encouraging diversification away from traditional dollar-denominated assets, according to Piggott.
Gold futures edged lower Monday as the U.S. dollar firmed, yields rose, and oil prices trimmed losses early in the day.
"The market remains caught in a tug of war between short-term selling pressure from macro-focused traders and demand from less interest-rate-sensitive investors seeking a safe haven amid multiple geopolitical and fiscal tensions," Saxo Bank analysts said in a note.
Investors are also awaiting next week's data on U.S. Personal Consumption Expenditures, the Federal Reserve's preferred gauge of inflation.
Traders now see an 82.8% chance that the Fed will leave rates unchanged this month, while expectations for a hike in December remain at 90%, according to the CME's FedWatch tool.
Front-month Comex gold XAUUSD for October delivery slipped 0.5% to $4,139.00/oz, and front-month Comex October silver XAGUSD lost two cents to $56.974/oz.DisclaimerContent provided by Seeking Alpha is intended for information purposes only, and that Seeking Alpha does not offer any personalist investment advice and is not a licensed securities dealer, broker, US investment adviser or investment bank.

articles.title: Gold edges higher as lower oil prices ease inflation concerns ahead of Fed meeting - Emirates 24|7
articles.summary: Gold edges higher as lower oil prices ease inflation concerns ahead of Fed meeting  Emirates 24|7
articles.full_text:
Gold prices gained modestly as easing oil prices reduced inflation concerns, while investors awaited the Federal Reserve’s rate decision and US inflation data
Reuters
Spot gold rose 0.2% to $4,172.87 per ounce by 1109 GMT. US gold futures for December delivery gained 0.3% to $4,193.30 per ounce. File picture used for illustrative purpose.
Washington: Gold prices edged higher on Monday as lower oil prices eased inflation concerns ahead of next week’s Federal Reserve monetary policy meeting, where the central bank is widely expected to keep interest rates unchanged.
Spot gold rose 0.2% to $4,172.87 per ounce by 1109 GMT. US gold futures for December delivery gained 0.3% to $4,193.30 per ounce.
“Lower oil prices are easing pressure on the Fed, which is supportive for gold. What is notable is that gold is holding up even as the dollar strengthens, as demand for safe-haven assets is benefiting both,” said UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo.
Oil prices slipped from a five-month high on Monday after US President Donald Trump waived sanctions and tariffs on Russia, a move that may lead to increased Russian fuel exports.
The drop in oil prices eased some inflation concerns following strong US CPI and PPI readings last week, driven in part by a surge in gasoline costs.
Investors are now awaiting next week’s Fed meeting and US PCE data, the central bank’s preferred measure of inflation.
“We expect the Fed to stay on hold this time, so the meeting itself may not be a major driver for gold. The key will be what the incoming inflation and labour-market data say about the path for rates,” Staunovo added.
According to CME’s FedWatch Tool, traders are pricing in only a 15% chance of a rate increase this month, while expectations for a December increase remain high at 89%.
While gold is typically considered a hedge against inflation, higher interest rates reduce the appeal of the non-yielding asset.
Elsewhere, the European Central Bank is likely to raise interest rates by 25 basis points at least once more this year to combat inflationary pressures, the International Monetary Fund said on Friday.
Among other metals, spot silver gained 1.2% to $57.6704 per ounce, platinum rose 1.3% to $1,652.22 per ounce and palladium climbed 2% to $1,134.25 per ounce.

The British pound has rallied to a four-week high as resilient UK employment data and hawkish Bank of England expectations support sterling ahead of today's inflation report. With a November BoE rate hike almost fully priced in, it may require an upside inflation surprise to provide another tailwind. GBP/USD bulls are eyeing a break above the 200-day EMA, while GBP/AUD shows signs of a potentially larger bullish reversal.

British Pound Strengthens Ahead of UK CPI as BoE Rate Hike Looms
UK Employment Resilience Keeps November BoE Hike on Track
The Bank of England (BOE) remains on track to hike in November after Tuesday's employment report provided further evidence of a resilient UK economy. Unemployment fell to 4.7% from 4.9% in September according to ONS, payroll employment rose by 13,000 in September, and regular wage growth reached 3.7% y/y, above expectations. That said, vacancies fell to 691,000, suggesting underlying labour demand remains subdued despite the headline improvement.
Money markets have almost fully priced in a 25bp hike to 4% on 5 November, with further tightening expected into 2027. BoE policymaker Megan Greene added to the hawkish narrative on Tuesday, warning that the risks of second-round inflation effects are greater than previously thought and reiterating the need for pre-emptive tightening. Her comments contrast with Governor Andrew Bailey's more cautious assessment that such pressures remain relatively subdued, highlighting divisions over how aggressively the BoE may need to respond.
Attention now turns to today's September CPI report, where headline inflation is expected to accelerate to 3.4% y/y from 3.1%. An upside surprise could reinforce sterling's interest-rate advantage, while softer inflation would challenge the extent of tightening currently priced into UK rates.
GBP/USD Technical Outlook: British Pound Eyes Further Gains
Sterling has rallied to a four-week high ahead of today’s inflation figures, fuelled by improving employment and wage data alongside scaled-back Fed rate bets. But GBP/USD bulls had to ride out a quick retest of the June low before the bullish reversal I hypothesised could get underway.
While resistance has been met around the 200-day EMA and 1.34 handle, the RSI (14) is back above 50 and nowhere near overbought. As we’re witnessing range expansion from a multi-week compression pattern at the end of a selloff, I suspect GBP/USD could have further to go to the upside. The RSI (2) warns of near-term exhaustion, though bulls may be seeking dips above 1.33 in anticipation of a break above the 200-day EMA.
Note the 1.3475 low and September VPOC at 1.3543 as potential upside targets for bulls.
Source: ICE, TradingView
GBP/AUD Technical Outlook: Inverse Head and Shoulders in Focus
Whether the inverted head and shoulders pattern on the weekly chart goes on to succeed remains to be seen, but it could take several weeks or months to play out if it does. Until then, I am focusing on whether we at least see the completion of the ‘right shoulder’ (RS) of the long-term bullish reversal pattern. This assumes a move higher towards the neckline around the June and March highs.
The daily GBP/AUD chart shows an explosive move out of a bull flag, though resistance was met around the 200-day EMA and monthly pivot point. Bulls could be seeking dips above the swing low around 1.859, though the monthly pivot point, high-volume node (HVN) and 1.90 handle also form a potential support zone to seek bullish reversal patterns.
Source: ICE, TradingView

articles.title: Billionaire Mukesh Ambani launches India’s biggest-ever IPO
articles.summary: Low-cost broadband provider Jio Platforms aims for £81bn valuation when it floats on the stock market on WednesdayIndia’s second-richest man, Mukesh Ambani, is launching what could be the country’s biggest-ever initial public offering (IPO), despite a stock market downturn.Mumbai-based Jio Platforms, a telecoms company backed by Meta Platforms and Google, is hoping to raise up to 302bn rupees (£2.4bn) and is targeting a 10.3tn rupees valuation when it floats on the stock market from Wednesday. C...
articles.full_text:
India’s second-richest man, Mukesh Ambani, is launching what could be the country’s biggest-ever initial public offering (IPO), despite a stock market downturn.
Mumbai-based Jio Platforms, a telecoms company backed by Meta Platforms and Google, is hoping to raise up to 302bn rupees (£2.4bn) and is targeting a 10.3tn rupees valuation when it floats on the stock market from Wednesday.
Set up a decade ago as a subsidiary of Ambani’s conglomerate Reliance Industries, and led by Akash Ambani, the oldest son of patriarch Mukesh, Jio offers low-cost broadband to millions of Indians.
Jio secured 212 anchor investors on Monday before its blockbuster IPO. They include some of the world’s largest fund managers, such as: BlackRock; Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund; the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority; Fidelity Investments; Schroders; JP Morgan Asset Management; Franklin Templeton; Invesco; and Prudential.
On Wednesday, shares will be offered to retail investors, and the IPO is set to close on Friday.
Reliance Industries said in a stock exchange filing last week that Jio had set a price range of 1,065 rupees to 1,119 rupees a share for its maiden share sale, offering up to 270m new shares.
The family-owned conglomerate has been encouraging its 400,000-plus employees to buy shares, offering them a discount of 54 rupees a share.
At the top end of the price range, Jio would be worth 10.3tn rupees, which would make it India’s fourth-largest company, behind its parent Reliance Industries, Bharti Airtel and HDFC Bank. It would be more than twice as much as the 4.9tn-rupee valuation in 2020, when Meta and Google invested in the company.
However, the top valuation is far below initial expectations of more than £110bn when the telecoms group posted a draft prospectus in the summer.
It comes amid a broader stock market slowdown in India, with the blue chip Nifty 5o index down more than 12% this year.
Jio launched its telecoms services in September 2016. It gained 16 million subscribers in the first month, and topped 100 million subscribers within 170 days, according to Reliance Industries. It is credited with making mobile internet more affordable, by triggering a price war. The company intends to expand further into artificial intelligence, cloud computing and digital infrastructure.
Isha Ambani, who sits on Jio’s board as a director, told investors last week that the business idea was spawned by the poor connectivity she and her brother Akash faced when they returned to India on a break from studying in the US in about 2009-10. She struggled to submit a college assignment online because the internet was not working.
“What followed was a conversation about why should India be left behind,” she said. “Akash firmly believed that the answer and solution to this was creating a digital technology platform company.”

articles.title: Yen Firms to 158.08 as Katayama’s Warning and Ueda’s 2% Inflation Signal Cap Dollar Below 160 - TradingNEWS
articles.summary: Yen Firms to 158.08 as Katayama’s Warning and Ueda’s 2% Inflation Signal Cap Dollar Below 160  TradingNEWS
articles.full_text:
Key Points
- USD/JPY fell 0.26% to 158.08, inside an October range of 156.95 to 158.95.
- Japan spent a record ¥15.4 trillion defending the yen from July 30 to August 26 with U.S. support.
- The BoJ holds rates at 1.25% against the Fed’s 3.75%–4.00%, a 250 to 275 bps gap.
USD/JPY traded at 158.08 in New York on Tuesday, down 0.418 yen, or 0.26%, from Monday’s close near 158.50. The pair dipped as low as 157.995 during the session as the yen gained in Asian trading, where Japanese authorities signaled they were closely monitoring currency moves. The yen held its gain through a volatile day for the dollar, even as Brent crude spiked to $111.75 before falling to $106.85. Over the past month, the yen has weakened 0.41% against the dollar. Over the past year, it has weakened 3.99%.
The thesis for this forecast is direct. USD/JPY is pinned in a narrow range because two powerful forces cancel each other out. On one side, a rate gap of 250 to 275 basis points between the Federal Reserve’s 3.75% to 4.00% range and the Bank of Japan’s 1.25% policy rate keeps the carry trade profitable and pushes the yen weaker. On the other side, Tokyo and Washington have shown they will buy yen in size when the pair approaches 160 to 164, having spent record sums this year to defend that zone. The result is a pair that drifts higher on carry and gets knocked back on official warnings. Risk is skewed toward a lower USD/JPY, because the upside is capped by intervention while the downside opens if the BoJ signals faster tightening.
The October range shows the trap. USD/JPY has traded between a low of 156.95 on October 2 and a high of 158.95 through mid-October. That 200-pip range is narrow for a pair that swung from 163.98 to 152.28 earlier this year. The 2026 high of 163.98 came in July, just before a coordinated U.S.-Japan intervention. The 2026 low of 152.28 came after it.
Tuesday’s move came on official signals. The yen strengthened past 158 per dollar last Thursday, reaching a one-week high after Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama warned that authorities were prepared to intervene again if necessary. She stressed that Washington and Tokyo’s position had not changed since their joint intervention in July. On Tuesday, the yen gained again in Asia as authorities said they were watching moves closely.
The calendar sets the timing. The Fed decides on October 28. The BoJ concludes its two-day meeting on October 30 and releases fresh quarterly growth and inflation forecasts. Those two decisions, 48 hours apart, will decide whether USD/JPY breaks out of its October range.
A 275 Basis Point Rate Gap Keeps the Carry Trade Alive
The interest rate gap is the main force pushing the yen weaker. The BoJ’s policy rate stands at 1.25% after a hike in September that followed an increase in June. The Fed’s target range sits at 3.75% to 4.00%. That leaves a gap of 250 to 275 basis points in favor of the dollar. At the long end, the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield traded at 5.10% on Tuesday, near the 5.31% peak of October 5, its highest in 24 years.
The carry trade turns that gap into steady yen selling. Investors borrow in yen at low rates and invest in dollar assets at higher rates, pocketing the difference. As long as the cost of money in Japan stays below the return available overseas, carry trades will reassert themselves after every intervention. A gap of 250 basis points is large enough that leveraged positions pay well even after an October BoJ hike.
The gap has been narrowing, which matters for the trend. Japanese officials have pointed out that the gap between Japanese and U.S. policy rates has been narrowing over time as the BoJ raised rates from 0.75% at the start of 2026 to 1.25% now. But the Fed has also been hiking. The Fed raised rates in September for the first time in three years, and fed funds futures price an 89% chance of another hike in December. If both central banks hike once more, the gap stays near 250 basis points.
U.S. inflation keeps the Fed tightening. September consumer prices rose 3.7%, above the 3.6% forecast. Producer prices jumped 6.3%. Those numbers raise the odds that the Fed holds its hawkish course, which keeps the dollar’s yield advantage intact.
The gap also explains why intervention has limited lasting effect. Intervention changes the quantity of yen available in the market, but it does not change the incentive to borrow or sell yen. After every round of official buying, the carry trade resumes because the underlying return differential has not moved. That is why the yen erased about half of its gains from the July intervention within two weeks.
For the forecast, the rate gap sets the baseline drift higher in USD/JPY. Without official resistance, the pair would likely trade above 160. The gap would need to narrow by 50 to 100 basis points before the carry trade loses its appeal, which would require either multiple BoJ hikes or a Fed pivot.
Tokyo Spent ¥15.4 Trillion Defending the Yen This Summer
The other side of the trade is Japan’s willingness to spend. Japan spent a record ¥15.4 trillion, about $98 billion, to support the yen between July 30 and August 26, according to its finance ministry. That followed a separate record ¥11.73 trillion deployed across April and May. In total, Japan has spent more than ¥27 trillion defending its currency in 2026.
The July operation was historic. For the first time since 1998, the United States joined Japan in a coordinated yen-buying operation. U.S. authorities, overseen by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, bought yen using their foreign currency holdings. The United States used euros rather than dollars to buy yen, which surprised markets. The motive appears to have been to avoid any need for Japan to sell U.S. Treasuries, as Japan is the world’s largest foreign holder of U.S. government debt.
The intervention worked at first. USD/JPY had crossed 163, its weakest level for the yen in four decades. After the coordinated operation, the pair fell to around 155, a yen gain of about 5%. Japan’s apparent line in the sand at 160 was defended.
The gains faded. Within two weeks, the yen had erased about half of the intervention’s effect, trading back above 159. By October it settled into the 157 to 159 range. Intervention scared markets but did not stop money from flowing to the higher-yielding currency.
The financing structure has changed. After the July operation, Japan’s finance minister said future dollar-selling intervention would be financed through the Fed’s Foreign and International Monetary Authorities repurchase facility, to avoid selling U.S. Treasuries outright. That arrangement gives Japan more firepower without disrupting the Treasury market, which makes future intervention more credible.
The scale matters for the forecast. A government that has already spent ¥27 trillion in a single year has shown it will act. Each intervention resets market psychology and makes traders cautious about pushing the pair toward the same levels. That caution caps USD/JPY below 160 even when the carry trade would otherwise lift it.
The intervention zone is well defined. The July operation was deployed near 162 to 164, and the April to May operation came at similar levels. Traders have learned that 160 is the warning line and 162 to 164 is where Tokyo acts.
Katayama, Mimura and Bessent Have Sent a “Very Clear” Message
The verbal warnings have been relentless. Japan’s top currency diplomat, Atsushi Mimura, said on September 28 that markets should take at face value the very clear message Tokyo and Washington had delivered on the yen, signaling his resolve to act against excessive falls. The yen spiked on his remarks, breaking through 157 to trade around 156.75. Asked whether Japan stood ready to intervene again, Mimura said he had nothing to comment on how authorities could act.
The message came from the top. Finance Minister Katayama said U.S. President Donald Trump raised concerns about yen weakness at a summit with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, an unusually detailed account of the leaders’ talks on currencies. Katayama and Bessent also reaffirmed in phone talks that the yen’s undervaluation was a concern.
Mimura has kept the pressure on. In early September, he said authorities were neither satisfied nor reassured by the yen’s moves and remained on a state of heightened alert. He declined to comment on whether authorities had conducted a rate check, the step officials usually take before intervening. That ambiguity is deliberate: it keeps traders guessing.
Katayama added her own warning last week. She said authorities were prepared to intervene again if necessary and that Washington and Tokyo’s position had not changed. The yen strengthened past 158 on her comments, reaching a one-week high.
Bessent’s position matters as much as Tokyo’s. He has said he believes the Japanese government and the BoJ would take action that leads to a stronger yen. He has also noted that a weakening yen could drag down other Asian currencies. Some read his call for Japan to sit back and enjoy the success of Abenomics as criticism of Takaichi’s large spending plans. U.S. participation means Washington views the yen’s weakness as a broader financial stability issue.
The verbal campaign has worked within limits. Each warning has pushed USD/JPY back by 50 to 150 pips. None has reversed the trend driven by the rate gap. The warnings keep the pair below 160, but they do not push it far below 157 on their own.
The credibility of the warnings rests on past action. Tokyo has intervened twice this year, once with Washington. Traders who test 160 do so knowing that the last two tests ended with the yen several yen stronger in days.

Oil Holds Its Risk Premium as Houthi Strikes Offset Russia Relief
Crude markets start the week with uncertainty after the US softened its stance on buying Russian oil, while the attack on Saudi’s energy facilities last weekend drew wider concern.
Brent: Saudi Supply in the Crosshairs
Yemen’s Houthi rebels claimed responsibility for multiple attacks over the weekend, including attacks on Saudi energy and airport infrastructure and the Shaybah oilfield. According to ING, the market remains at risk premium due to the heightened war risk.
Russian supplies are also coming under increased pressure. A series of drone attacks by Ukraine over the weekend set fire to an oil terminal and a nearby depot in St. Petersburg. The terminal, according to Kpler, exports approximately 120,000 bpd of refined petroleum products.
However, the other way on the scale is President Trump’s executive order from Friday, which removed sanctions and tariffs relating to Russia, including penalties on countries buying Russian energy.
WTI: Inventories Back in Focus
Inventories are likely back in focus for WTI after a week of solid gains last week. The Cushing stock build last week was smaller than expected and markets will now look toward EIA inventory data for further insight.
A Reuters poll showed crude and products stockpiles are expected to have dropped last week. Data shows US stockpiles have been declining over the last couple of weeks, which keeps the focus on domestic supply ahead of the EIA’s report this week. The Nov WTI contract expires on Tuesday.
Natural Gas: Mild Weather Versus Record LNG Pull
On Monday, expectations for milder weather cut forecasts for heating demand, which countered bullish factors like small storage builds, lower production and LNG demand. On average, LNG feedgas has been at 18.1 bcfd. Lower 48 production averaged 111.3 bcfd.
Two opposing factors influenced the gas and LNG market this week. LNG feedgas hit a new high at 20.7 bcfd. Meanwhile, Columbia Gas restored 1.9mn Dth/d of capacity, bringing supply back to Appalachia. While that has increased supply in the US, the attack on ships in the Middle East has limited global LNG supply, making it more difficult for Europe to restock for the winter.
Natural Gas Technical Analysis: NG Slips Below $3.03 as $2.97 Support Comes Into Focus
Natural gas is currently trading at around $3.01/MMBtu, and what’s notable is the sustained selling following last week’s triangle breakdown. The most recent bounce ended at $3.09 and price has fallen below the previous support of $3.03 and $3.05. The moving averages are both falling, and the faster moving average is still below the slower moving average, which keeps the short-term trend bearish.
The first major support I’m looking at is at $2.97. If that support is breached, then $2.91 would be the next support and that would also be a breakdown of the previous uptrend that started from the early October lows. If that happens, then $2.87 would be the next support.
Resistance is at $3.03, $3.09 and $3.15. The RSI is at 34, and still bearish. A recovery above $3.03 would also negate the bearish case, and so would a move above $3.09. I would also add that if $3.09 is broken, then a more serious move to the upside could take place. From there a return to $3.15 would still be in the realm of possibility.
WTI Technical Analysis: USOIL Holds $98.09 as $99.72 Remains the Key Breakout Test
WTI crude is at $98.67 on the 1 hour chart. On the upward channel from mid-October, the price has tested lower levels and been defended by the lower level of the channel. Twice the price has tried to break out at $99.72 and has formed a double top with the last high from October 10th. For now, the price is above both moving averages.
$99.72 is the first major resistance. If this breaks, $100.86, and the channel upper level, would be the next target. $98.09 and the lower channel line would provide support, followed by $97.65. Even lower $96.73 and $95.34 would provide support.
RSI is at 55 and falling, signaling that a drop may occur, but the lower level of the channel continues to be defended, so a drop may be short-lived.
If $98.09 and the channel lower level is defended, I would view the outlook as slightly bullish. A break of $99.72 would provide a better outlook. A close below $96.73 would flatten the channel.
Brent Technical Analysis: UKOIL Holds $109.97 as $111.07 Comes Into Focus
Brent is trading at $109.92 as of the 1-hour chart. What I find important is how strongly the breakout from the contracting triangle held. The previous resistance at $107.00 to $107.57, which rejected price 3 times, has since turned to support. A rising trendline is also supporting the lows, while both moving averages are still far from price and are pointing up.
The first resistance I am looking at is $111.07, where the last leg of the move higher stopped. Breaking through that would bring $112.08 into play. Supporting the move lower would be the $109.97 pivot level, then the rising trendline and $108.83. Further down, the $108.14 level and the previous breakout of $107.57 would come into play.
RSI is at 59, and is headed lower, and has slipped just below the signal line at 62. That suggests bullish momentum and a mild uptrend is still in place. However, that may change if price breaks below $108.83.
I am leaning slightly bullish, and would expect $108.83 to act as support. I would also expect $111.07 to be a stiff resistance, and possibly a breakout level to the upside. A close below $107.57 would bring the contracting triangle into question.

articles.title: UK unemployment falls as payrolls stabilise; Deutsche Bank sees November rate hike - Yahoo Finance UK
articles.summary: UK unemployment falls as payrolls stabilise; Deutsche Bank sees November rate hike  Yahoo Finance UK
articles.full_text:
UK unemployment fell to 5% in the three months to August as payroll employment returned to growth, adding to signs that the labour market may be stabilising.
Official figures showed employment increased by 102,000 over the quarter to 34.6 million, while economic inactivity edged down to 21%.
Payroll employment rose by 13,000 in September, its strongest monthly increase since August 2025, although the total remained 66,000 lower than a year earlier.
Wage growth also remained firm, with regular pay rising 4% year on year and total pay increasing at the same rate.
Public-sector regular pay increased 6%, compared with 3% growth in the private sector.
However, vacancies fell by 21,000 to 691,000 in the three months to September, showing that demand for workers remains subdued despite the improvement in employment measures.
Deutsche Bank chief UK economist Sanjay Raja said the figures reinforced evidence that the labour market is beginning to stabilise after a prolonged slowdown.
He said the improvement should support government tax receipts, while stronger employment and wage growth suggested less spare capacity in the economy than previously thought.
For the Bank of England, Deutsche Bank said the data strengthened the case for another interest-rate increase, particularly with inflation expected to move above 4% in the coming months.
Unless Wednesday's inflation figures deliver a significant downside surprise, Raja said a November rate hike now looks increasingly likely.

articles.title: Why are FIIs selling Indian stocks in 2026? Rs 3 lakh crore outflow amid crude oil surge, rising US bond yields and weak Rupee - ET Now
articles.summary: Why are FIIs selling Indian stocks in 2026? Rs 3 lakh crore outflow amid crude oil surge, rising US bond yields and weak Rupee  ET NowFPIs pull out 52,100cr from Indian equities in October so far  The Times of India11 years, zero net FII flow: How a $64 billion outflow erased 9 years of equity buying  The Economic TimesFIIs net sell Rs 1,149 crore-worth Indian equities, lowest outflow of October; DIIs net buy Rs 3201 crore  Moneycontrol.comNeelkanth Mishra...
articles.full_text:
Foreign investors have pulled Rs 49,457 crore out of Indian equities in October so far, the third-biggest monthly net selling of 2026, according to NSDL data as of October 19. Over the past 10 months, FIIs have net sold Rs 3.09 lakh crore of Indian stocks. The churn out is likely on the back of a surge in crude oil prices, which held near $108.3 a barrel, as renewed fighting across West Asia heightened concerns over supply disruptions.
Now, if we look at the foreign institutional investors (FIIs), they're not getting much out of Indian stock markets, compared to what other emerging markets are providing. For example, the Korean benchmark, Kospi, has given a return of more than 31per cent year-to-date; Japan's Nikkei 225 has surged 27 per cent during the same time frame; the Chinese benchmark index, Shanghai Composite Index, fell 6.6 per cent YTD. Compare it with the Indian benchmark Nifty50, which has declined over 12 per cent YTD. 
Not just that, foreign investors have been selling in Indian equity markets due to rising US Bond yields, contracting the spread with India's G-Sec yield. 
Narrowing US and India 10-year yield 
The yield on the 10-year US Treasury note rose as much as 5.3 per cent recently, staying at its highest level since 2007 as expectations strengthened that the Federal Reserve would tighten monetary policy further to contain inflation.
The narrowing yield gap is central to the shift. India’s 10-year G-Sec yield is at 7.37 per cent, while the US 10-year climbed to as much as 5.12 per cent. The spread has narrowed to about 225 basis points, from around 500 basis points during the Covid-19 period.
How does it affect Indian markets? US Treasury bonds are considered one of the safest investments in the world. Investors see them as a risk-free rate of return. When Treasury yields rise, investors can earn a higher "risk-free" return.
So, a 5 per cent return from a safe US bond is better than a 10-12 per cent expected return from Indian equities with much higher risk. As the yield gap narrows, some investors shift money from emerging market stocks like India to US Treasuries. 
India’s foreign exchange reserves declined by nearly $60 billion in six weeks to $726.027 billion as of October 9, from a record high of $785.706 billion on September 4. The fall was largely attributed to the Reserve Bank of India’s intervention to support the rupee amid rising crude oil prices, higher US yields, and sustained foreign investor outflows.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) uses the U.S. dollar as its primary intervention instrument to manage the rupee under a managed floating exchange rate regime.

articles.full_text:
Earlier, gold prices continued to fall slightly during the trading session on October 20th as investors assessed the likelihood of the US Federal Reserve (Fed) continuing to raise interest rates this year, ahead of its monetary policy meeting next week.
By the end of yesterday's trading session, spot gold prices had fallen 0.3% to $4,125.90 per ounce; while December gold futures closed down 0.4% at $4,142.60 per ounce.
Gold prices remain approximately 26% lower than their record high of $5,594.82/oz set in January and around 22% lower than at the start of the Iran conflict, as concerns about inflation fueled by rising energy prices have reinforced expectations that the Fed will continue to raise interest rates.
Bob Haberkorn, senior market strategist at StoneX, commented: “Inflation and the Fed’s interest rates are currently the two biggest factors putting pressure on gold prices. At this point, US government bonds seem more attractive than gold as a safe-haven asset.”
According to Haberkorn, the $4,000/oz level is a crucial price point to watch in order to assess the ability of gold to maintain its support. The price movement at this level currently depends largely on policy signals from the Fed.
Following a 0.25 percentage point interest rate hike in September, marking the first increase of 2026, the Fed faces differing expectations regarding its policy trajectory in the remaining months of the year. Recent statements from Fed officials suggest there is no urgent need to further tighten monetary policy, thus reducing expectations of a rate hike at the October 27-28 meeting.
However, the market still forecasts a high probability of the Fed raising interest rates again in December. According to CME Group's FedWatch tool, traders currently assess the probability of the Fed raising interest rates in December at 92%.
Gold has traditionally been seen as a hedge against inflation, but its appeal diminishes in a high-interest-rate environment because it does not yield returns.
Besides the Fed's policy decision, investors are also awaiting the US Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index data, expected to be released next week. This is the Fed's preferred measure of inflation, and it could provide further signals about the persistence of price pressures and the outlook for interest rate adjustments.
In Japan , Bank of Japan (BoJ) Governor Kazuo Ueda said that core inflation has moved fairly close to the 2% target, suggesting there is still room for further interest rate hikes.
Technically, according to Kitco's analysis, the nearest resistance zone for spot gold is between $4,147 and $4,176 per ounce. If it breaks through this zone and maintains its upward momentum, the price of gold could head towards $4,201 per ounce and then the recent high around $4,218 per ounce.
On the downside, the $4,119/oz level was identified as the first support level. However, gold prices fell below this level during the morning trading session on October 21st. The next support levels to watch are $4,100/oz and further down at $4,074/oz.

articles.summary: Bond market turmoil complicates ECB rate decision  The Irish Times
articles.full_text:
The European Central Bank (ECB) has raised interest rates twice in the last four months and another hike is expected in December as the bank combats the surge in inflation from energy prices.
That was the holding narrative we’ve been working from for the past number of weeks, but there’s a new weave in the tapestry that is complicating matters.
Turmoil in bond markets is lifting borrowing costs independently of the ECB’s rate hikes, which is also cooling the economy. The bond sell-off and commensurate surge in yields is reducing the need for further rate hikes, placing a question over whether the ECB will opt for a December rate hike.
Carsten Brzeski, global head of macro at ING, says the context has changed since September. “The surge in German bond yields since the September meeting has already had roughly the same impact on growth and inflation as an additional 25bp [basis points] rate hike,” he said.
READ MORE
“For France, it’s closer to a 50bp hike. With bond markets doing the ECB’s job, some central bank officials might be less keen to continue hiking than they were at the September meeting.”
ECB chief Christine Lagarde said pretty much the same thing on Saturday, noting that the current bond sell-off was making borrowing more expensive in the euro zone, curbing economic growth and ultimately inflation.
“While growth has been resilient, financing conditions have tightened, with long-term interest rates rising notably since our last meeting,” Lagarde told fellow central bankers and finance ministers gathering in Bangkok.
“This will slow growth and reduce pass-through by more than projected in our September exercise.”
If the ECB opts for a further quarter-point bump in December, that would take the bank’s policy rate to 2.75 per cent, a level financial officials define as restrictive or curtailing of economic activity.
The inflation outlook, and the second-round impacts on food and other items (which have yet to materialise) is being closely monitored.

articles.title: French 10-Year Bond Yield Nears 5% as Stocks, Bonds and Currency Selloff Rattles Eurozone - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: French 10-Year Bond Yield Nears 5% as Stocks, Bonds and Currency Selloff Rattles Eurozone  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
French financial markets are enduring a rare simultaneous strain on stocks, bonds and the currency. Hit by a double blow from violent riots in multiple cities over the weekend and the uncertain outlook for the 2027 budget, the yield on France's 10-year government bonds rose as high as 4.93% early this week, approaching the 4.99% reached in early October—the highest level since 2002. At the same time, the spread between French and German bonds of the same maturity widened to 146 basis points, the CAC 40 fell 1.5%, and the euro weakened against the dollar, the pound and the yen alike.
The trigger for the selloff came from the streets. Over the weekend, protests over rising living costs and deteriorating public services escalated into violent riots in multiple French cities, with shops looted and public buildings damaged in Paris and elsewhere. French President Emmanuel Macron described the situation as "shameful and infuriating." The scale of the unrest exceeded the government's expectations, putting both social order and fiscal pressure on the table at once.
The bond market promptly repriced France's fiscal risk. On Friday, the yield on 10-year French government bonds (OATs) closed at about 4.78%, with the spread over German bunds of the same maturity at roughly 137 basis points; by Monday, yields had climbed further and the spread had widened to a two-week high. By comparison, the yield on 10-year Italian BTPs rose 11 basis points over the same period to 4.58%, suggesting the pressure has begun to spill over to other highly indebted eurozone economies.
| Indicator | Recent Level | Key Milestone | 
|---|---|---|
| French 10-year bond yield | 4.93% (Monday) | 4.99% in early October, highest since 2002 | 
| French-German 10-year spread | 146 basis points | Monthly high of about 159–160 basis points | 
| French 10-year bond CDS | About 82 basis points | 89 basis points on October 2 | 
| CAC 40 index | Down 1.5% in one day | Weaker than the roughly 1% drop in the STOXX Europe 600 | 
Note: Data reflect market levels early this week; yields and spreads fluctuate with trading.
In equities, France was the worst performer among major European markets. Shares of BNP Paribas and Société Générale both fell about 3%, leading the decline; the retail sector also came under pressure, with Carrefour down 1.8%. Its chief executive said the company would suffer losses in the tens of millions of euros from protest-related damage. Sovereign credit default swap (CDS) premiums rose about 5 basis points, the worst-performing sovereign CDS in Europe on the day.
The euro at one point fell 0.5% to $1.1183, ranking last among G10 currencies. The cost of hedging against further euro depreciation climbed noticeably, reflecting traders' continued bearish stance on the outlook.
The root of the market pressure is that France's finances offer almost no win-win option. To ease the protests, the government needs to spend more on living costs, education and public services; to stabilize the bond market, it must rein in deficits and debt. French public debt has reached nearly 120% of gross domestic product, and the finance ministry expects government debt interest costs to exceed €90 billion (approximately $101.2 billion) next year—more than planned spending on defense and education. The 2027 budget the government is pushing contains about €43 billion (approximately $48.4 billion) in deficit-reduction measures, but securing a compromise in a deeply fractured parliament was already difficult, and with only about six months until the presidential election, the challenge is even greater.
Asset manager Ninety One warned that if the 2027 budget fails to pass, France's fiscal deficit could exceed 6% of GDP next year—more than double the EU's 3% ceiling. Sahil Mahtani, director of the firm's investment research institute, said a new parliamentary election could follow next year's presidential vote, and if parliament continues to lack a clear majority, uncertainty over the budget and fiscal policy could persist into 2028.
The pension system is seen as the toughest nut to crack. Charlotte de Montpellier, senior economist for French economic research at ING, noted that if France truly wants to improve its debt dynamics, it needs to reform a pension system whose costs are significantly higher than in other countries—but such a policy is highly unpopular politically.
The minority government led by French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has asked some local authorities to impose curfews, stepped up security deployments and offered aid to damaged businesses, but the fiscal situation limits room to quell public discontent through large-scale new spending.
The response from across the Atlantic has been relatively calm. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday that he does not expect the turmoil in the French bond market to have broad spillover effects, adding that France faces a severe situation but that Macron's economic team is highly capable. He noted that safe-haven flows from some troubled countries into US Treasuries have already emerged, with the US 10-year Treasury yield down about 20 basis points from its early-October high.
Financial institutions, however, are not letting down their guard. Vanessa Holtz, head of European securities and country head for France at Bank of America, said the bank is closely watching the situation in France, especially how far the protests might escalate and whether stability can be restored quickly; political and fiscal uncertainty is prompting investors to be more selective about French assets, with the market increasingly focused on asset quality.
Louis-Vincent Gave of Gavekal Research offered a gloomier assessment: "France today is simultaneously facing a social crisis, an immigration crisis, an energy crisis, an economic crisis and a fiscal crisis." He sees nothing in what happened over the weekend that points to a stronger euro or lower French bond yields.
On the ratings front, Moody's plans to review France's sovereign credit rating this Friday (October 23). Given its negative outlook, a downgrade is seen as the more likely next step; Moody's currently rates France one notch above Fitch and S&P Global. Analysts at Commerzbank believe the move would merely bring Moody's in line with the other agencies, and the negative impact of a downgrade on the spread could be fairly limited.
For investors, the core question is whether France's risk premium will continue to widen. Elias Hilmer, a market economist at Capital Economics, expects the French-German 10-year spread to widen from about 140 basis points currently to 200 basis points by the end of 2027, while spreads of most other eurozone countries over Germany may narrow over the same period. The firm also cautioned that if the rise in French bond yields stems mainly from genuine market concerns about its public finances rather than a broad malfunction in the eurozone bond market, it may be harder for the European Central Bank to intervene directly.
This means that in the window before the 2027 budget and the presidential election, France's ability to execute fiscal policy will be priced more directly into bond yields and the French-German spread, and the risk stratification of eurozone assets may deepen accordingly.

The UAE benchmark rate for 24-carat gold declined to AED 497.00 per gram from AED 500.50 the previous day. The price of 22K gold fell to AED 460.25, extending its retreat from the higher levels recorded in late September.

At the current benchmark rate, 10 grams of 24K gold would cost approximately AED 4,970, while the same quantity of 22K gold would cost AED 4,602.50.
These calculations exclude making charges, retailer premiums and any applicable taxes. Final jewellery prices can therefore differ between stores even when the underlying gold rate is the same.
The decline in local prices followed weakness in the international bullion market. Spot gold slipped approximately 0.1% to $4,136.46 per ounce during early Asian trading as higher government-bond yields reduced demand for non-interest-bearing assets.
US gold futures also traded near $4,139 per ounce as the dollar strengthened and Treasury yields moved higher. The combination is normally negative for bullion because a stronger dollar makes gold more expensive for buyers using other currencies, while rising yields increase the opportunity cost of holding an asset that pays no interest.
The UAE dirham’s peg to the US dollar means domestic gold prices generally track movements in dollar-denominated international bullion closely. As a result, changes in US interest-rate expectations can quickly affect rates in Dubai, Abu Dhabi and other emirates.
The Federal Reserve will hold its next policy meeting on October 27 and 28. Investors broadly expect policymakers to leave the federal funds rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4.00%, although recent inflation data have strengthened the argument for additional tightening later in the year.
Market pricing indicated an approximately 85% probability that the Fed would keep rates unchanged in October. Expectations for a December rate increase remained much stronger, reflecting concerns that inflation could stay above the central bank’s target.
The policy outlook became more uncertain after US consumer inflation accelerated to 3.7% in September, exceeding the 3.6% consensus forecast. Producer prices subsequently jumped 1.3% month over month and 6.3% from a year earlier, with energy costs accounting for a substantial part of the increase.
Higher inflation can affect gold in two opposing ways. Persistent price growth may increase demand for bullion as an inflation hedge. However, it can also encourage the Fed to keep rates higher or raise them further, supporting the dollar and bond yields while creating short-term pressure on gold.
For the moment, the interest-rate effect appears to be dominating.
The 10-year US Treasury yield was trading around 5.09%, remaining near historically elevated levels even after retreating from a recent peak of approximately 5.31%.
Higher long-term yields increase the relative appeal of government bonds compared with gold. Investors can earn interest from Treasurys, whereas returns from bullion depend entirely on price appreciation.
Gold could recover if the Fed signals that it is comfortable pausing for an extended period. A softer policy message would probably place downward pressure on yields and the dollar.
Conversely, any warning that another increase could arrive in December may keep UAE gold rates under pressure, particularly if upcoming US economic figures remain strong.
Despite the current pullback, geopolitical and fiscal risks continue to provide support for the longer-term gold market.
Uncertainty surrounding Middle East energy supplies has kept oil prices elevated, increasing concern that higher fuel costs could feed into global inflation. Investors are also monitoring government borrowing, political instability in Europe and the sustainability of US fiscal policy.
These risks may preserve demand from central banks and long-term investors even if high interest rates produce further near-term volatility.
For UAE buyers, this creates a mixed outlook: gold could remain under pressure before the Fed meeting, but safe-haven demand may limit the scale of any decline.

articles.title: Institutions warn of diminishing efficacy of rate hikes, leaving the Bank of England’s next interest rate decision at an impasse - Moomoo
articles.summary: Institutions warn of diminishing efficacy of rate hikes, leaving the Bank of England’s next interest rate decision at an impasse  Moomoo
articles.full_text:
Against the backdrop of diverging global monetary policies and persistently rising energy inflation, the Bank of England's policy choices are becoming increasingly complex. Lloyds Banking's latest warning gets to the heart of the dilemma: by following the Federal Reserve in raising interest rates, the UK may no longer be able to bolster the pound, leaving policymakers facing a costly and largely ineffective standoff.
With the supportive effect of interest-rate hikes waning, sterling's performance has become mixed.
Lloyds Banking has made it clear that rising UK interest rates can no longer provide the sterling with the same effective boost as in the past. Karim Henide, the bank's rate strategist, stated that if the UK simply follows the Federal Reserve Chair's policy trajectory, it will only bear the economic costs of tightening without achieving any relief at the exchange-rate level.
On Tuesday (October 13), during Asian trading hours, the pound staged a modest rebound against the U.S. dollar, currently hovering around 1.3215—near a three-month low—with gains of roughly 0.2%. Meanwhile, the pound held steady at 1.1835 against the euro, close to this year's peak.
Lloyds Banking still believes that a rate hike by the Bank of England in November is highly likely.
The exchange-rate transmission mechanism has shifted, and the effectiveness of policy is steadily waning.
Enid further noted that in the past, tightening monetary policy in the UK effectively bolstered the pound, but this effect has weakened considerably in recent years. A weaker exchange rate continues to push up domestic import prices, putting upward pressure on inflation. He illustrated this with data: between 2017 and 2019, a 10‑basis‑point increase in Bank of England interest rates was enough to lift the pound against the U.S. dollar by roughly 1.5%; since 2022, however, the same magnitude of rate hikes has had virtually no meaningful impact on the exchange rate.
He argues that a 1% depreciation of the pound would push UK inflation up by roughly 7 basis points over two years, and further currency weakness would make it increasingly difficult to maintain a policy of inaction. However, the benchmark interest rate's influence on the exchange rate has diminished considerably; raising rates would not only increase borrowing costs for households and businesses but also fail to deliver the same benefits in terms of lower import prices as in the past.
Market Expectations and Policy Mismatch
Enid noted that the bond market appears to be overlooking the UK's more challenging trade-off between economic growth and inflation. According to model-based estimates, under a strict inflation-targeting framework and in line with mainstream economic forecasts, the optimal average policy rate for the Bank of England by 2027 would be around 4.2%; by contrast, if the Monetary Policy Committee were to disregard the initial energy shock, that level would fall to approximately 3.5%, significantly below the current market-implied rate of 4.59%. It should be emphasized that these results are conditional projections based on annual averages, rather than definitive year-end rate forecasts.
The logic underpinning this market‑based pricing assumes that Brent crude oil will average around $125 per barrel throughout 2027. Enid explicitly emphasized that one key reason raising interest rates has become ill‑timed is the policy's lag. The tightening effects of rate hikes typically only fully materialize after inflation has already declined substantially, thereby significantly increasing the risk that longer‑term inflation falls below target. In scenario simulations, the current pricing trajectory is projected to lower inflation by roughly 0.3 percentage points by the fourth quarter of 2028—albeit at the cost of a 0.38‑percentage‑point rise in the unemployment rate.
Lloyds Banking also identified a deep-seated contradiction: a pronounced misalignment between market expectations for interest rates and those for inflation. Market‑based inflation swaps suggest that, even after the anticipated rate hikes, price pressures will remain more persistent than model forecasts predict. Enid acknowledged that market pricing is signaling that tightening policies may be ineffective, a view he shares given that current demand‑side tools are ill‑suited to address supply‑side inflationary pressures.
Concerns about energy‑related inflation remain unabated, constraining the Bank of England's policy flexibility.
If costly energy prices continue to spill over into wages and the prices of other goods, it will severely constrain the Bank of England's room for inaction. Enid notes that the extent to which the Monetary Policy Committee can preserve policy flexibility hinges largely on the pass‑through effects of energy prices. Historical experience suggests that the UK has typically exhibited stronger second‑round inflationary transmission than the United States, providing a compelling rationale for not dismissing the initial energy shock outright.
Notably, at its September meeting, the Bank of England decided to keep the benchmark interest rate unchanged at 3.75%. In its statement, the bank also noted that there are currently no signs that second-round inflationary effects have become pronounced; however, if energy prices remain elevated for an extended period, the associated risks could intensify. The next interest-rate decision is expected to be announced on November 5.
Conclusion
In summary, the pound's trajectory will be a key determinant of the Bank of England's policy flexibility. A strong exchange rate can provide the central bank with a buffer against external tightening pressures, whereas a weak pound will compel it to adopt a more hawkish stance—even if such rate hikes can no longer bolster the currency as they did before 2022.
In today's complex and volatile global macro environment, markets are closely watching how the Bank of England navigates the delicate balance between curbing inflation and maintaining exchange-rate stability.

Several of India’s biggest IPOs, including those of Hyundai Motor India, LIC and Paytm, delivered weak or modest listing gains. Jio Platforms may break that pattern: anchor investors showed strong demand and its grey market premium points to a potential premium.
Reliance Jio IPO Review | All You Need To Know About The Biggest Indian IPO
India’s primary market has seen several big-ticket IPOs struggle to deliver strong listing gains, leaving investors cautious about whether large offerings can translate into immediate market rewards.
With Jio Platforms’ much-awaited IPO set to open tomorrow, in what could be the country’s biggest-ever initial public offering (IPO), the key question is whether the Reliance Industries-backed digital business can buck the trend and deliver a strong debut.
So far, eight of the 13 IPOs with issue sizes exceeding ₹10,000 crore, including the recently listed NSE, have made relatively modest stock market debuts. The National Stock Exchange of India listed at a premium of just 0.84% over its issue price.
The ₹27,858 crore IPO of Hyundai Motor India witnessed a muted listing in October 2024, with the shares debuting at ₹1,934 apiece against the issue price of ₹1,960.
The listing of Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC), the country’s largest life insurer, was also disappointing for investors. In May 2022, LIC made a weak debut on the exchanges, with its shares listing at ₹867.20, an 8.62% discount to the issue price of ₹949.
The journey of the Rs18,300 crore IPO of One 97 Communications, the parent company of Paytm, has been marked by sharp twists and turns since the fintech major’s listing in November 2021. Paytm shares debuted on the exchanges at ₹1,950, a 9.3% discount to the IPO price of ₹2,150 apiece.
LG Electronics India was a major outlier, with its shares listing at a massive 50% premium over the issue price, marking the biggest listing gain among big-ticket IPOs in this comparison.
What are the Street’s expectations from Jio Platforms’ IPO?
Street expectations for Jio Platforms have been high since the company filed its draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) in June. The offering marks the first public issue from the Reliance group in nearly two decades and the first consumer-facing business within the conglomerate to go public.
The strong response from anchor investors on Monday and the elevated grey market premium (GMP) indicate that the telecom and digital services giant could break the trend of muted listings.
Jio Platforms allotted shares worth ₹8,109.85 crore to 212 anchor investors at the upper end of its price band, after institutional demand for the offering exceeded ₹2.5 trillion, or more than 30 times the amount available in the anchor book, according to a stock exchange filing and people familiar with the matter.
The anchor investors include some of the world’s largest fund managers and institutions, such as BlackRock, Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund, the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, Fidelity Investments, Schroders, JPMorgan Asset Management, Franklin Templeton, Invesco, and Prudential.
Jio Platforms IPO GMP rises to ₹260
The grey market premium (GMP) for Jio Platforms’ proposed initial public offering (IPO) has attracted attention as the issue opening date approaches. As of Tuesday, the GMP stood at ₹260, according to market sources, indicating a potential listing premium of around 23% over the upper end of the issue price band of ₹1,119.
Grey market trends are unofficial and can change before the IPO opens. They do not necessarily reflect the IPO’s final valuation or actual listing performance. The final issue price is determined by the company in consultation with its merchant bankers after considering multiple factors.
