articles.title: Index Funds Increase Emerging-Market Bond Outflow Risk - CEO Magazyn
articles.summary: Index Funds Increase Emerging-Market Bond Outflow Risk  CEO Magazyn
articles.full_text:
Investors in emerging-market government bonds increasingly follow global benchmarks rather than basing investment decisions primarily on each country’s economic conditions. By the end of 2025, benchmark-linked investors held USD 464 billion in local-currency sovereign bonds, representing 42.8% of foreign portfolios, according to research by Serkan Arslanalp, Stijn Claessens and Daniela Klingebiel presented by the Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR).
USD 464 billion in benchmark-linked portfolios
Foreign investors in the sample held USD 1.084 trillion of emerging-market local-currency government bonds at end-2025. Of this, USD 464 billion was held by investors linked to the J.P. Morgan GBI-EM Global Diversified index and USD 620 billion by other investors.
In 2004, the corresponding amounts were just USD 2 billion and USD 45 billion respectively. The benchmark-linked share of foreign holdings increased from 16.9% in 2010 to 42.8% in 2025. China’s inclusion in the index in 2020 and India’s in 2024 helped expand benchmark-linked assets sevenfold. Their share of the entire local-currency government bond market increased more modestly, from 2.8% in 2012 to 3.7% in 2025. The non-benchmark share fell from 11.1% to 5%.
Global risk and the dollar drive portfolio shifts
The researchers examined how different investor categories react to market conditions. For benchmark-linked investors, global factors represented by the VIX volatility index and a broad US dollar index accounted for more than 90% of the variation explained by their model.
For other foreign investors, domestic factors — the bilateral exchange rate and sovereign credit rating — accounted for nearly 75% of explained variation. These investors responded more directly to the economic conditions and creditworthiness of individual countries.
A one-standard-deviation increase in VIX was associated with a 2.1% fall in benchmark-linked holdings, while a comparable strengthening of the dollar was associated with a 1.3% decline. For other investors, a one-standard-deviation depreciation of the local currency corresponded to a 1.9% reduction in exposure, while a comparable credit-rating improvement was associated with a 1.8% increase.
Non-benchmark investors do not consistently offset outflows
Although non-benchmark investors held portfolios around one-third larger than those linked to indices at the end of 2025, the researchers found no consistent pattern of increased purchases when index-linked capital exited emerging markets. Domestic non-bank investors also did not systematically offset global episodes of risk aversion. Domestic central banks and commercial banks were more likely to act against the prevailing market direction and absorb some foreign selling.
This helps explain why even countries with strong macroeconomic fundamentals can face exchange-rate and bond-market pressure when global portfolio managers reduce exposure to emerging markets as an asset class.
Local-currency debt and the new form of original sin
Historically, the term original sin described emerging economies’ difficulty borrowing abroad in their own currencies. Dollar-denominated debt made depreciation raise the domestic cost of debt service. Growth in local-currency bond markets has reduced this direct mismatch but has not eliminated exposure to international capital flows.
The concept of original sin redux captures the risk that foreign investors sell debt issued in local currency when global risk increases, pushing bond prices lower, yields higher and the exchange rate down — even if domestic fundamentals have not deteriorated.
How China and India changed index weights
Adding China and India to the benchmark reduced some existing countries’ weights, though the effect on each domestic bond market also depends on which securities qualify for the index. Eligibility varies with issue size, maturity, liquidity and foreign-investor access.
The eligible share of a domestic bond market ranged from approximately 11% in Turkey to 93% in Peru. Before the inclusion of China and India, benchmark investors held 31.2% of Peru’s local-currency sovereign bond market but just 3.2% of Brazil’s, despite Brazil’s much larger index weight.
In a simulation keeping benchmark assets unchanged, China and India’s inclusion reduced Brazil’s weight by 3.28 percentage points, but its domestic benchmark-investor share by only one point. Peru’s index weight declined 0.91 point, translating into a 7.2-point drop in benchmark holdings relative to its local market. The equivalent decline was 7.1 points for Romania and 6.7 points for the Czech Republic.
Country caps amplify exposure for smaller issuers
The J.P. Morgan GBI-EM Global Diversified index currently caps each country’s weight at 10%, with the limit scheduled to fall to 9% by January 2027. Capping larger issuers redistributes weight to smaller eligible markets.
The researchers estimate a redistribution multiplier of approximately 2.07 under the 10% cap and 2.32 under the 9% cap for eligible bonds. This can make smaller countries relatively more exposed to simultaneous withdrawals during global shocks.
The authors recommend greater transparency in benchmark changes, publication of simulated weights ahead of adjustments, and consideration of transition costs. Public-debt managers should regard index eligibility as one part of managing their investor base, rather than an objective in itself.
Source: CEPR research by Serkan Arslanalp, Stijn Claessens and Daniela Klingebiel, 2026.

articles.title: Gold Price Forecast: XAU/USD at $4,134 as Record 4,256-Tonne ETF Holdings Meet 5.10% Yields — $4,360 Target - TradingNEWS
articles.summary: Gold Price Forecast: XAU/USD at $4,134 as Record 4,256-Tonne ETF Holdings Meet 5.10% Yields — $4,360 Target  TradingNEWS
articles.full_text:
Key Points
- Global gold ETF holdings hit a record 4,256 tonnes in September, despite an 8.5% monthly price drop.
- China’s central bank bought 23 tonnes in September, its biggest monthly purchase since October 2023.
- The 10-year Treasury yield at 5.10% caps gold near $4,200, with December Fed hike odds at 89%.
Spot gold (XAU/USD) traded at $4,134.60 per troy ounce at 11:29 a.m. in New York on Tuesday, down $5.30 on the day. The session range ran from a low of $4,110.80 to a high of $4,156.30. December COMEX futures traded at $4,165.40, up $5.30, or 0.13%, after opening at $4,162.40. The gap between spot and futures, $30.80, reflects carry costs at a time when short-term rates sit well above 4%. Gold has spent October trapped between last week’s low of $4,073 and high of $4,217, and Tuesday’s tape kept it near the middle of that range.
The thesis for this forecast is direct. Physical and official buyers are building a floor at $4,100 while leveraged futures sellers and a 10-year Treasury yield above 5% are capping the market at $4,200. Global gold ETF holdings hit a record 4,256 metric tons in September, even as the price fell 8.5% that month. China’s central bank bought 23 tonnes in September, its largest monthly purchase since October 2023. Against that, hedge funds cut their net long futures exposure by $12 billion, and the 10-year yield sits at 5.10% to 5.14%. Gold is caught between buyers who hold metal and sellers who trade paper.
The longer view explains why the market is cautious. Gold sits 23.5% below its $5,405 record. It traded at $4,360 a month ago and at $4,316 a year ago, which puts it 5.2% lower over a month and 4.2% lower over a year. September’s 8.5% decline was the heaviest monthly loss of the cycle, and the October bounce has not recovered it.
Tuesday’s drivers pushed in both directions. Brent crude spiked to $111.75 in the morning, a five-month high, on Houthi attacks against Saudi infrastructure and mines in the Strait of Hormuz. Higher oil revives inflation fears, which revives Fed hike bets, which pressures a non-yielding metal. Gold fell to $4,110.80 as Brent spiked. When Brent rolled over toward $106, gold recovered to $4,134.60. The relationship is inverted from the textbook: on this tape, higher oil hurts gold because it means higher rates.
The calendar is now the main driver. The Federal Reserve meets October 27 and 28, and core PCE inflation lands on October 29. Fed funds futures price an 82% chance of a hold in October and an 89% chance of a hike in December. Gold’s next $100 move depends on which of those numbers shifts first.
Record 4,256 Tonnes in ETFs While the Price Fell 8.5%
The single most important data point for gold right now is the divergence between price and physical holdings. Global gold ETF holdings rose by 67 metric tons in September to a record 4,256 tons. During the same month, the London benchmark price fell 8.5%. Investors added metal into the sell-off rather than redeeming it.
That breaks the pattern of the first eight months of 2026. For most of the year, ETF holdings tracked price closely. They fell during the correction from the January high and recovered as gold rebounded through August. In September the two lines split. Holdings reached 101.3 million ounces on October 8, up 5.3% from the July low of 96.2 million ounces, while price traded between $4,100 and $4,200.
The second quarter showed the opposite behavior. ETF investors sold 44.8 tonnes of gold in the quarter as prices fell from their highs. The turn from net selling in the second quarter to record holdings by the end of the third quarter marks a shift in investor behavior. Funds that had been reducing exposure into weakness are now adding.
The geography of the buying matters. Asian-listed funds accounted for almost half of the increase in global holdings over the 12 months to September. U.S.-listed funds contributed 30% and European funds 20%. Gold’s marginal buyer is increasingly in Asia, and that demand responds to local conditions, including weak stock markets and falling bond yields, rather than to U.S. rate expectations.
The limit of this support is clear from September itself. ETF purchases of 67 tonnes did not stop an 8.5% decline. Physical demand cushions a fall but does not prevent one when the futures market is selling. Leveraged futures positions, not long-term ETF holders, set the marginal price in the short run.
That is the core tension in the forecast. The ETF data says investors are building positions at $4,100 to $4,200. The futures data says traders are reducing them. When the two diverge, the futures market wins on any given day, and the ETF market wins over a quarter. Gold’s floor at $4,100 is built by the ETF buyers. Gold’s ceiling at $4,200 is built by the futures sellers. The record holdings argue that the floor is more durable than the ceiling.
China Bought 23 Tonnes in September, the Most Since October 2023
Official sector demand is the second pillar under gold, and China is leading it. The People’s Bank of China reported a 23-tonne purchase in September, its largest monthly addition since October 2023. September marked the central bank’s 23rd consecutive month of reported buying. China’s official gold holdings reached 2,410 tonnes, equal to 8.5% of total reserves, after 103 tonnes of additions since January.
The timing of China’s buying is the signal. The PBoC stepped up its purchases through the third quarter and accelerated in September, the month gold fell 8.5%. A central bank that buys more as prices drop is a price-insensitive buyer. That is the definition of a floor, though not an unbreakable one.
Chinese investors followed the official lead. Chinese gold ETFs posted inflows of 11 tonnes in September, their third consecutive monthly gain, lifting total holdings to a month-end record of 304 tonnes. Over the third quarter, Chinese gold ETFs took in $3.9 billion, adding 27 tonnes and lifting total assets under management by 13%. Those inflows offset second-quarter losses and put Chinese gold ETFs on course for a record year of inflows.
Three forces are driving the Chinese bid. Domestic equities have been weak, which pushes savers toward alternatives. Chinese government bond yields have kept falling, which lowers the income investors give up by holding gold. And the central bank’s repeated purchase announcements have encouraged private buyers to follow. ETF demand carried into early October as local investors kept diversifying away from stocks.
Jewelry is the weak spot. Consumer jewelry demand in China has struggled at current prices, and the divergence between investment buying and jewelry buying shows that gold is being bought as a reserve and portfolio asset rather than as a consumer good. Holiday demand for jewelry, bars and coins did improve as prices moderated in early October, with domestic prices hovering around RMB 900 per gram and the international benchmark holding above $4,100.
The local price action confirms the support. The Shanghai benchmark fell 5.5% in yuan terms during September, against 8.5% for London. Chinese buyers absorbed part of the global sell-off, and the narrower decline in Shanghai reflects that demand.
For the forecast, China is the most important source of support below $4,100. A central bank buying 23 tonnes a month at these prices is unlikely to stop if gold drops another 3%.
Central Banks Bought 288.9 Tonnes in Q2, and Kazakhstan Is the Exception
China is not buying alone. Central banks globally purchased 288.9 tonnes of gold in the second quarter, up 62% from a year earlier. First-half official buying reached 345 tonnes. Net official purchases came in at 39 tonnes in August. The second quarter is the clearest example of the split in gold demand: ETF investors sold 44.8 tonnes while central banks bought 288.9 tonnes, more than six times as much.
The annual pace is slowing but remains heavy. Central banks bought 863 tonnes in 2025, and the 2026 total is expected to come in below that figure. Projections earlier in the year pointed to 850 tonnes. Even at a slightly lower pace, official demand removes the equivalent of several months of mine supply from the market each year.
Official demand behaves differently from investor demand. Central banks buy on long horizons and are far less sensitive to price. When speculators or ETF holders sell, official buyers tend to absorb the supply rather than follow the trend. That makes official demand the part of the gold market least likely to leave when sentiment turns, and it is why the $4,000 to $4,100 zone has held through the October volatility.
Kazakhstan is the exception. The National Bank of Kazakhstan plans to cut gold’s share of its international reserves from 78% to 75% by year-end, after its holdings climbed to 386 tonnes. Kazakhstan was the world’s fourth-largest reported central bank buyer through August, adding 36 tonnes in the first eight months of the year. The planned reduction is a rebalancing exercise driven by gold’s large weight in the country’s reserves, not a sign that official demand is reversing broadly.
Rebalancing sales of that kind matter at the margin. A reduction from 78% to 75% of reserves, depending on the size of the total reserve pool, could release a modest number of tonnes onto the market before year-end. Against China’s 23 tonnes in a single month, that supply is small.
The broader motivation for official buying has not changed. Reserve managers have been diversifying away from reliance on any single asset, and the dollar’s share of global reserves has been a long-running concern. With U.S. federal deficits running at $1.992 trillion for fiscal 2026, outlays of $7.396 trillion against receipts of $5.403 trillion, that concern is unlikely to fade. Official demand is the slowest-moving force in the gold market, and it is pointing up.

articles.title: Ahead of massive IPOs, AI companies are sketching plans to share their wealth - Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: Ahead of massive IPOs, AI companies are sketching plans to share their wealth  Yahoo FinanceInvesting in the public benefit  AnthropicElon Musk and Dario Amodei Are Offering Gifts—With Strings Attached  The AtlanticSpaceX, Anthropic plan to share wealth with the public amid concern AI could trigger job losses  Los Angeles TimesWhat to Know About the Obscure Trust Looming Over Anthropic’s IPO  WSJ
articles.full_text:
NEW YORK (AP) — As they steam toward massive public offerings on Wall Street, the companies at the forefront of artificial intelligence have begun sketching plans to share their wealth with the public — a commitment they say is imperative to address disruptions the technology could bring to the workforce and people's livelihoods.
Executives at Anthropic and OpenAI have long argued the technology's arrival will bring many benefits for everyday people, and they've promised that will include a share of the profits. The companies are outlining a range of proposals for distributing AI fortunes, but so far they have not resolved key questions over how they would work, how transparent they will be, and who will determine beneficiaries.
On Sunday, Anthropic said it would commit 5% of its shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new entity within the company, pending approval from stockholders. The stake could increase "as the company grows" in the future. The maker of AI assistant Claude said the fund "might explore" larger donations to traditional nonprofits or potentially distribute money to "specific populations."
The San Francisco-based company shared little information about the types of organizations supported by the fund and the issues they will address. One area it will not support, Anthropic said, is lobbying and political giving.
Phil Buchanan, the president of The Center for Effective Philanthropy, said he welcomed Anthropic's commitment — especially at a time when he said some billionaires are "diminishing the importance of philanthropy." But he cautioned that Anthropic should avoid the "arrogance" of previous technology barons who assumed their professional expertise would translate to philanthropic wisdom.
Buchanan recommended the fund support highly effective, existing nonprofits but said it is "hard to talk about any of this because it's all so abstract."
"I guess I'm hopeful," Buchanan said, "but I'm not going to get too excited until I see some evidence of what's actually happening."
Anthropic's pledge hinges on Wall Street plans
Anthropic, which was valued at close to $1 trillion earlier this year, is preparing for an initial public offering as soon as next month that is shaping up as one of the biggest ever.
Once a company is public, donations might be made through the selling of future shares, or potentially turning to cash dividends in the future, explained Jay R. Ritter, director of The IPO Initiative at the University of Florida's Warrington College of Business. The specifics on how charitable donations will be made through Anthropic's fund are not clear yet.

articles.full_text:

A Reuters survey found 94 of 100 economists expect the Fed to hold rates at 3.75%–4.00% in October, while all 100 forecast a December hike as inflation remains elevated. Persistent rate-hike expectations and rising yields could weigh on Bitcoin and other crypto assets by reducing demand for riskier investments.
Key takeaways
- 94 economists expect Fed rates unchanged in October
- All 100 surveyed forecast another December interest-rate hike
- Persistent inflation strengthens expectations of tighter monetary policy
The Federal Reserve is widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged at its October 27-28 meeting, but economists now overwhelmingly anticipate another increase in December as persistent inflation complicates the central bank's policy outlook.
A Reuters survey conducted October 16–20 found that 94 of 100 economists expect the Fed to maintain its benchmark interest rate at 3.75%–4.00% this month.

articles.title: Fed Expected to Hold Rates in October Before December Increase - Finance Monthly
articles.summary: Fed Expected to Hold Rates in October Before December Increase  Finance Monthly
articles.full_text:
The Federal Reserve is expected to leave US interest rates unchanged in October before raising them again in December, according to a Reuters poll of economists concerned about persistent inflation and the strength of the American economy. The survey, conducted between October 16 and 20, found that 94 of 100 economists expect the central bank to maintain its benchmark interest rate at 3.75%–4.00% when policymakers meet on October 27–28. All 100 respondents anticipate an increase in December, compared with fewer than half in the previous month's survey.
The shift follows the Federal Reserve's unanimous decision to raise rates by 25 basis points in September, its first increase since 2023.
Inflation remains the central concern. Higher energy prices linked to the conflict involving Iran, alongside tariffs on imported goods, have increased pressure on household budgets and business costs. Oil prices remain above $100 a barrel, adding to concerns that inflation could remain elevated for longer than previously expected.
Economists surveyed by Reuters forecast that the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index, the Fed's preferred inflation measure, will remain more than one percentage point above its 2% target over coming quarters. The survey suggests inflation may not return to target until at least 2028. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh has avoided signalling how policymakers will vote at their next meeting, despite growing expectations of another increase before the end of the year. The uncertainty has contributed to volatility in US government bond markets.
Longer-term Treasury yields climbed to multi-decade highs earlier in October before retreating as expectations of an immediate rate increase weakened. For investors, further monetary tightening could affect bond prices, equity valuations and the attractiveness of different asset classes. Higher interest rates also create challenges for borrowers.
Mortgage rates, business financing costs and consumer credit could remain elevated if monetary policy stays restrictive into 2027. Companies with floating-rate debt or refinancing requirements may face additional pressure on profitability and investment plans. Despite these concerns, the US economy has demonstrated considerable resilience. Economic growth reached an annualised 2.2% in the second quarter, supported partly by investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure. Economists expect growth of approximately 3.2% in the third quarter before moderating to 2.2% during the final three months of 2026. Annual economic growth is forecast at 2.3% for 2026 and 2.1% in 2027. Consumer spending has also remained relatively strong, although some economists believe the resilience is concentrated among higher-income households benefiting from financial market gains. The combination of economic growth and persistent inflation has raised questions about how far interest rates may need to increase.
Nearly 60% of economists surveyed expect the benchmark rate to peak at 4.00%–4.25%. However, 38 of 92 respondents anticipate at least two further increases, compared with approximately one-fifth in September. The October meeting takes place shortly before the US midterm elections, adding political attention to a decision already closely watched by financial markets.
For investors and borrowers, the distinction between October and December is increasingly important. An October pause would not necessarily signal the end of monetary tightening. Instead, it could give policymakers additional time to assess inflation and economic conditions before deciding whether another increase is justified.
The December decision will provide a clearer indication of how aggressively the Federal Reserve intends to respond to persistent price pressures.

articles.title: The Model Assistant in action: What would an escalating Iran war mean for bond yields? - Oxford Economics
articles.summary: The Model Assistant in action: What would an escalating Iran war mean for bond yields?  Oxford Economics
articles.full_text:
In Part 1 of this series, we introduced the AskOEAI Model Assistant, the world’s first AI assistant for scenario modelling, and explained why we built it. In this post, we put it to work on a question many of our clients are asking right now: what would a renewed escalation of the war in Iran mean for the global economy, and for government bond yields in particular?
The question: what if the war in Iran escalates again?
The war in Iran has already pushed up energy prices and unsettled financial markets. Renewed attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure in the Gulf have lifted oil prices, and global bond markets have sold off sharply. The US 10-year Treasury yield has climbed above 5% for the first time since 2007, and the Federal Reserve raised interest rates in September for the first time since 2023, as we discuss in our latest analysis of the bond sell-off.
Our baseline forecast already reflects the conflict and the market moves seen so far. What many clients want to know is what happens if the war escalates again: how far could energy prices rise, how would inflation and central banks respond, and how much higher could bond yields go? So we asked the Model Assistant, walking through four simple steps:
- Describe your scenario in your own words, as broadly or as specifically as you like.
- Research the scenario with the assistant, drawing on Oxford Economics’ analysis to propose shocks, their timing and the reasoning behind each.
- Review and adjust inputs as required, then run the scenario through the GEM with a single click or message.
- Analyse the results through charts and explanations, then refine your assumptions and re-solve as often as you need.
Describe the scenario in your own words
We started with a single prompt: “Model a scenario of new and sustained escalations in the war in Iran”
We didn’t specify any indicators, shock sizes or timings. In its first response, the assistant pulled in the most relevant Oxford Economics research and set out a complete first draft of the scenario.
The assistant based its calibration on the downside case from our research on a prolonged Iran war, which points to sustained energy disruption, higher inflation risk premia and increased long-term borrowing costs. It translated these channels into four shocks, starting in Q4 2026 (Table 1).
Table 1: Scenario inputs proposed by the Model Assistant
| Input | Assumption | Rationale | 
| Brent crude oil price | +$37 from 2026Q4-2027Q4 | The elevated oil price path supported by prolonged-war downside case | 
| European gas price | +$5 from 2026Q4-2027Q4 | Sustained LNG disruption and tighter European supply | 
| Asian gas price | +$10 from 2026Q4-2027Q4 | Asian LNG markets’ greater exposure to prolonged disruption | 
| Supply chain stress | +1.0 from 2026Q4-2027Q4 | Sustained disruption to shipping, logistics and refined-fuel movements | 
Source: Oxford Economics AI Model Assistant
Each input comes with a short rationale and a preview chart showing how the scenario path compares with our baseline.
Run the scenario and review the results
Once we’re happy with the inputs, a single click on Solve runs the scenario through the GEM. The shocks feed through trade, prices, financial markets and policy responses across economies, and the results are automatically benchmarked against our latest baseline.
Once the scenario had solved, we asked for the impact on US yields, and the assistant returned a chart and a short summary. In our scenario, US 10-year government bond yields are 0.78 percentage points above baseline at their widest gap, in 2028Q2. Higher energy prices and supply-chain stress create inflation pressure and prompt a tighter monetary policy stance, keeping risk premia elevated, lifting yields and tightening financial conditions.
Understand what is driving the results
The assistant’s analysis pointed to a tighter monetary policy stance as a key factor behind the initial rise in yields. To understand this better, we asked the Model Agent: “How does the Fed react?”
Based on our initial assumptions, the assistant gave a concise description of the Fed’s “stagflationary trade-off”, along with further research to review. Higher inflation creates pressure to raise rates, while weaker growth and a softer labour market subsequently lead to rate cuts. This Taylor-rule mechanism drives policy-rate dynamics in the GEM, but users can take their own view and add a new assumption.
Refine the scenario through conversation
A scenario is rarely complete in one go. Having reviewed the results, we assumed a more hawkish Fed reaction: “Assume the Fed is more hawkish, raising rates by 50bps above the baseline until the energy shock subsides.”
The assistant added a fifth shock, raising the US policy rate by 0.5 percentage points above baseline from 2026Q4 to 2027Q4, until the energy shocks fade.
Adding the assumption means solving the scenario again, which takes a single click, and each version is traceable in the chat.
With a more hawkish Fed, US bond yields rise more quickly and stay higher for longer than in our first run. Comparing the two gives a range of ‘what-if’ outcomes under different assumptions, all built through conversation with the Model Assistant.
From economic question to modelled insight
In four steps, we went from a topical question to a fully modelled scenario grounded in our research, complete with charts and an explanation of the results. We didn’t need to know which variables to shock, by how much, or how to set up the model inputs. Every assumption was transparent and open to change, so we could question the results, adjust the shocks and re-solve within the same conversation.
The Model Assistant is designed to make scenario analysis quicker and open to more people, with economic judgement staying firmly with the user. To find out more about the problem it solves and what sets it apart from general-purpose AI tools, read part 1 of the series.

articles.title: Will the Fed Raise Interest Rates Again This Month? - Norada Real Estate Investments
articles.summary: Will the Fed Raise Interest Rates Again This Month?  Norada Real Estate Investments
articles.full_text:
If you're buying a home or thinking about refinancing, that mix matters more than the headline. Let's walk through it.
Will the Fed Raise Interest Rates Again This Month? What the Odds Say Now
Here's the short version. The Fed raised rates once in September and is expected to sit tight in October. Most of the hiking talk has moved to the December 8–9 meeting. Still, a 1-in-7 chance of a surprise is not zero.
Where the Fed Funds Rate Stands Right Now
At its September 15–16 meeting, the Fed raised the federal funds rate by 0.25 percentage point to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%. The new range took effect on September 17. It was the Fed's first rate hike in three years, and the vote was unanimous.
Before that, the rate had been parked at 3.50% to 3.75% all year. So September was a clear change in direction. The question is no longer when the next cut comes, but how many more hikes are on the way.
What Markets Are Betting On for October 28
Markets put real money behind their best guess. On Kalshi, a prediction market, the “Fed maintains rate” contract is trading at about 87%, while a quarter-point hike sits near 13%. A rate cut is basically off the table at under 1%. Fed funds futures, which many traders watch, tell a similar story, with roughly 84% to 86% odds of a hold.
Right after the September hike, some investors expected back-to-back hikes. That idea has faded. The bigger bet now is a quarter-point hike in December, not October.
Why Chair Warsh Isn't Giving Any Hints
Don't expect the Fed chair to tell you what's coming. Speaking at the IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok on Friday, October 16, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh made it clear he isn't going to preview the decision.
“I don't prejudge meetings,” Warsh said. “I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year.”
He also said, “It's a new chapter at the Fed,” and that the Fed is “not in that business anymore.” In other words, no more hinting at the next move weeks ahead of time. For you, that means fewer clues before the announcement. Most people read that as leaving the October pause in place.
The Inflation Problem the Fed Can't Ignore
Inflation is the reason a hike is even on the table. The Consumer Price Index rose 0.6% in September, and prices were up 3.7% over the past 12 months, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That's up from 3.4% in August and still nearly double the Fed's 2% goal.
Energy did most of the damage. Gasoline jumped 9.1% in September and drove more than half of the monthly increase. Core inflation, which leaves out food and energy, rose 0.3% for the month and 2.6% for the year.
That split is why the Fed may hold off for now. If most of the pain comes from gas prices, officials may want to see whether it fades first. If it spreads into everything else, the pressure to act grows fast.
What the September Minutes Told Us
The minutes from the September meeting, released on October 7, gave us the clearest look at the Fed's thinking. According to the minutes, “most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year end.”
Note the words “by year end.” With two meetings left in 2026, that leaves room to wait until December. Officials also said they “approached each meeting with an open mind.”
Several officials also called the current rate “not restrictive or only mildly restrictive.” In plain English, some of them don't think today's rates are slowing the economy much yet. That's a quiet warning for anyone hoping rates have peaked.
What Could Change the Fed's Mind Before October 28
Odds can move fast in the final week. A few things could make a surprise hike more likely:
- More bad inflation news: Any fresh sign that price increases are spreading beyond gas and energy would make the Fed nervous.
- A strong jobs picture: If hiring and wages stay hot, officials may worry that demand is fueling inflation, not just energy shocks.
- Rising inflation expectations: If people and businesses start expecting higher prices to stick, the Fed tends to act sooner.
Softer data or calmer energy prices would lock in the pause.
What This Means for Mortgage Rates
Here's something a lot of people mix up: the Fed doesn't set mortgage rates. It sets a short-term rate banks use to lend to each other overnight. Mortgage rates tend to follow the 10-year Treasury yield, which moves on inflation worries and what investors expect the Fed to do over time.
That's why mortgage rates are already high even though the Fed has only raised rates once this cycle. The 10-year Treasury yield was 5.09% on October 16, according to the U.S. Treasury. The average 30-year fixed purchase rate is 7.14% today, according to Zillow, and Freddie Mac's weekly survey put it at 7.40% for the week of October 15.
If the Fed Holds
A pause is mostly priced in, so don't expect mortgage rates to drop just because the Fed sits still. The bigger mover will be the tone of the statement and Warsh's press conference. A calm tone could help rates ease a little. A tough one could push them up even with no hike.
If the Fed Surprises With a Hike
A surprise hike would likely jolt bond markets and push mortgage rates up quickly. In real numbers: on a $400,000 loan, a 30-year fixed at 7.14% costs about $2,699 a month in principal and interest. At 7.39%, just a quarter point higher, it's about $2,767. That's roughly $68 more every month, or more than $24,000 over the life of the loan.
Should You Lock Your Mortgage Rate Now or Wait?
There's no single right answer here. A rate lock is like a restaurant reservation. You hold your table at today's price, even if the place gets busier tomorrow. Here's a simple way to decide.
Lean toward locking now if:
- You're under contract and closing within the next 30 to 45 days.
- Your monthly budget is tight, and a $50 to $100 jump would hurt.
- You'd lose sleep watching rates bounce around before the October 28 decision.
It may be OK to wait if:
- You're still shopping for a home and haven't made an offer yet.
- Your lender offers a float-down option that lets you grab a lower rate if one shows up.
- You have room in your budget to handle a rate that drifts a bit higher.
Thinking about a refinance? If your current rate is well under 7%, you likely won't come out ahead right now. If it's well above today's offers, ask your lender how long it takes to win back the closing costs. If that's longer than you plan to stay, it's probably not worth it yet.
My Take on the Weeks Ahead
My read is that the Fed holds in October and keeps December wide open. With inflation at 3.7%, the data isn't friendly, so mortgage rates are likely to stay near 7% for now, with some bumps around the October 28 announcement.
Don't try to time the Fed perfectly. Focus on what you can control: your credit score, your down payment, and quotes from at least three lenders. Buy the home that fits your life and budget. If rates fall later, you can look at refinancing then. The right move is the one that fits your situation, not this week's headlines.

Vale CEO Sees Long-Term Balance in Iron Ore Market Despite China Steel Decline
The global iron ore market is expected to stay balanced over the long term as worldwide demand keeps growing even with lower steel output in China, according to Platts. Gustavo Pimenta, chief executive of Brazilian mining company Vale, offered that assessment at the FT Metals & Mining Summit held in London from Oct. 14 to 16.
Pimenta attributed the balanced outlook to ongoing depletion in the iron ore sector, estimating annual depletion at roughly 60 million to 80 million tons. In his view, the Simandou mine in Guinea, which is projected to reach a production capacity of as much as 120 million metric tons per year by 2030, will mainly help offset that depletion while also supporting demand for ultra-clean ore.
Ore from Simandou carries a higher alumina content, an impurity in steelmaking. Pimenta said this raises Vale's importance as a corrector of the entire system, meaning the company's low-alumina products become more sought after when blast furnace feeds with poorer chemical characteristics must be blended with high-purity material.
Pimenta also indicated that Vale is unaffected by the decline in China's crude steel production. According to the World Steel Association, Chinese crude steel output fell 3.1 percent year over year to 651.9 million metric tons over January through August 2026. Pimenta described China as a very important market and pointed to what he called massive growth in the country's manufacturing sector.
On copper, Pimenta said Vale has the highest growth among major producers, with output of about 380,000 metric tons and a target of 700,000 metric tons, mostly from Carajas in Brazil, at very low capital intensity. He noted that one of Vale Base Metals' two projects under construction has half the capital intensity of a typical greenfield development, helped by existing rail, port and other infrastructure in Brazil and by the quality of the natural resource endowment.
With that development in the pipeline, Pimenta expects Vale Base Metals' contribution to the company's EBITDA to rise to 40 percent from 30 percent.

articles.title: POSCO-backed Port Hedland HBI project in Australia receives federal environmental approval - SteelOrbis
articles.summary: POSCO-backed Port Hedland HBI project in Australia receives federal environmental approval  SteelOrbis
articles.full_text:
The Australian federal government has announced that it has granted environmental approval for the Port Hedland Iron Project – Stage 1, backed by South Korean steelmaker POSCO, Japan-based Marubeni and Taiwan's China Steel Corporation.
The approval was issued to project developer Port Hedland Iron Pty Ltd on October 7, 2026, under the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999 and remains valid until June 30, 2088. The project must commence within five years of the approval date, by October 7, 2031, unless the approval conditions are amended. The Western Australian government previously granted final state-level approval for the approximately 3 billion project in April 2026.
Port Hedland facility to produce 2 million mt of HBI annually
The project will be developed in the Boodarie Strategic Industrial Area, approximately 10 km southwest of Port Hedland in Western Australia's Pilbara region.
The planned facility will include an iron ore processing complex, a pellet plant and a hot briquetted iron (HBI) production facility, consuming approximately 3-3.5 million mt of iron ore annually. Most of the pellets produced will be used internally to manufacture approximately 2 million mt of HBI per year, while around 700,000 mt of pellets will be exported through Port Hedland.
Project to utilize MIDREX technology
The facility will utilize MIDREX direct reduction technology, using natural gas instead of coal to reduce greenhouse gas emissions compared to conventional blast furnace-based ironmaking. It will also include hydrogen production and storage facilities to support processing operations and longer-term decarbonization objectives.
Construction of the Port Hedland Iron Project is expected to take approximately 2.5 years, while the project's operational lifespan is estimated at up to 101 years.

articles.title: OpenAI Speeds Up Fundraising Before Rival Anthropic’s Upcoming IPO - WinBuzzer
articles.summary: OpenAI Speeds Up Fundraising Before Rival Anthropic’s Upcoming IPO  WinBuzzer
articles.full_text:
- Funding Race: OpenAI is reportedly seeking about $30 billion in investment commitments before rival AI developer Anthropic’s expected November stock-market debut.
- Capital Delivery: SoftBank completed an earlier $30 billion OpenAI investment on October 1, paying its final $10 billion installment.
- Revenue Dispute: OpenAI challenges Anthropic’s revenue accounting as investors weigh the rivals’ valuations; Anthropic says it follows established practices.
OpenAI is pushing to secure about $30 billion from investors before rival artificial intelligence developer Anthropic’s expected mid-November stock-market debut, Reuters reports. The ChatGPT maker is seeking commitments while the two companies approach increasingly overlapping backers, competing over where those investors allocate their money.
The proposed round could value OpenAI above $1.4 trillion. SoftBank and Abu Dhabi-based investment fund MGX are among existing backers in talks to participate, according to the people cited by Reuters. OpenAI and SoftBank declined comment for the report; Anthropic and MGX did not immediately respond.
Overlapping Backers Face Two Financing Offers
OpenAI met investment funds, including sovereign wealth funds that invest state assets, in the week before the report, while Anthropic hosted its own investor day. Reuters’ sources described a process moving unusually quickly for a round of this size, with investors evaluating competing offers within days or weeks.
MGX was also an investor in Anthropic’s May funding round, when the Claude developer raised $65 billion.
Anthropic’s May funding round valued it at $965 billion, including the new investment. A public offering would give investors another opportunity to buy into the company, which many critics see as extremely overvalued and possibly facing a risk of bancruptcy, an outlook it shares with OpenAI. Anthropic expects to spend at least $518 billion on AI infrastructure over roughly a decade.
Kroll Bond Rating Agency (KBRA) assigned Anthropic a BB+ rating (speculative grade / high-yield “junk” rating, one notch below investment grade) in June 2026 covering portions of its junior and senior chip debt.
Anthropic submitted a confidential draft registration for an initial public offering to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on June 1. Its announcement made the offering conditional on the regulator’s review, market conditions and other factors.
Reuters reported strong demand for shares in both developers. Some investors nevertheless saw OpenAI’s accelerated effort as a way to secure money that funds might otherwise allocate to Anthropic’s offering.
Financial Disclosures Could Change the Comparison
One person cited by Reuters said OpenAI wanted to finish fundraising before Anthropic’s financial disclosures gave investors a fuller view of its business. Those disclosures could bring demands for more detail from OpenAI chief financial officer Sarah Friar about its own revenue growth and outlook.
Edward Best, co-chair of capital markets at law firm Willkie Farr & Gallagher, suggested OpenAI might prefer to establish its valuation before facing a competitor comparison.
OpenAI’s pitch includes an annualized revenue figure of $50 billion and an expectation of reaching $70 billion by the end of 2026, according to Reuters’ sources. Annualized revenue projects a recent sales pace over a full year.
The controversial accounting method also changes the number investors see. OpenAI deducts partners’ shares when recording revenue and has accused Anthropic of inflating its figures by counting the full value of contracts sold through outside cloud providers. Anthropic’s response to that criticism was that it follows established accounting practices.
On October 8, the Financial Times reported that investor documents put OpenAI’s annualized revenue near $50 billion at the end of September. A person responding through CNBC said an earlier $68 billion estimate included gross revenue from partnerships, to make comparison with Anthropic easier.
Anthropic told investors third-quarter revenue reached $16.8 billion, up from $11.6 billion in the second quarter, while slowing monthly growth raised concerns. After Anthropic’s quarterly results fell short of expectations, some existing and prospective investors favored an IPO valuation nearer $1.5 trillion rather than the $2 trillion the company sought, Reuters reported.
Earlier Commitments Still Finance OpenAI
OpenAI’s March funding round closed with $122 billion in committed capital at an $852 billion valuation including the investment. Committed capital can arrive in installments.
SoftBank paid the final $10 billion installment of an earlier $30 billion OpenAI investment on October 1 through Vision Fund 2, its investment vehicle. It financed that payment with proceeds from issuing senior notes, a form of debt.
Investors familiar with OpenAI told Reuters the company needs capital for infrastructure commitments and to strengthen its finances if weaker IPO markets further delay its planned 2027 listing.

articles.title: Ringgit ends flat as investors await Fed decision - Free Malaysia Today

articles.title: AI trading sentiment deteriorates, storage chip stocks decline in pre-market trading - KuCoin
articles.summary: AI trading sentiment deteriorates, storage chip stocks decline in pre-market trading  KuCoin
articles.full_text:
Tech stocks declined again as earnings season for major tech companies approaches, continuing to pressure AI-related trades. Meanwhile, the dollar weakened, and the market entered a wait-and-see mode.
Pre-market in the U.S. on Tuesday, memory chip stocks declined broadly: SK Hynix fell about 4%, Western Digital dropped around 2%, SanDisk slid about 2%, Micron Technology declined about 2%, and Seagate Technology fell about 2%. The Korean Composite Stock Price Index dropped 3.7%, becoming one of the deepest-lowering major indices in Asia-Pacific, with chip giant SK Hynix down 4.23%, nearing its lowest closing price since April. The MSCI Asia Pacific Index fell 1.4%, sharply diverging from Monday’s U.S. tech-led rally. Nasdaq 100 futures declined 0.4%, and European stocks are expected to open 0.7% lower.
This week, tech giants such as Meta and Tesla released their earnings reports in quick succession, leaving investors generally cautious due to lingering doubts about whether AI-related investments can sustain their upward momentum. On the same day, data center infrastructure company Elice Inc. plunged over 33% on its first day of trading in Seoul, further dampening market confidence in emerging cloud service-related stocks.
HSBC’s chief economist, Frederic Neumann, said: “The relief-driven rebound in U.S. tech stocks overnight failed to spread to Asian markets. Investors remain in risk-off mode, with rising bond yields and persistent energy prices as key concerns. Market doubts about the sustainability of the AI asset rally continue to linger, as higher financing costs increase the risk of project delays or cancellations.”
Pre-market in U.S. equities, memory chip stocks declined broadly: SK Hynix fell about 4%, Western Digital dropped about 2%, SanDisk slipped about 2%, Micron Technology declined about 2%, and Seagate Technology fell about 2%. The Nikkei 225 closed down 1.3% at 64,075.42. The Tokyo Stock Price Index (TOPIX) ended down 1.4% at 4,009.21. The South Korean KOSPI Composite Index closed down 3.7% at 5,552.74. The spot U.S. dollar index fell 0.2%; the yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury note decreased 2 basis points to 5.12%; the yield on Japan’s 10-year government bond rose 1.5 basis points to 2.920%; the euro advanced 0.2% to $1.1231; gold declined 0.5% to approximately $4,120 per ounce; and Brent crude oil rose above $110.20 per barrel.
Earnings season becomes a critical test for AI trading
This week, major tech companies will release their earnings reports in quick succession, directly testing the strength of the rally in AI-related stocks. Netflix Inc. will report earnings on Tuesday, followed by Tesla, Meta, and IBM Corp. the next day.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose 1.6% on Monday, ending its longest eight-day losing streak since 2008 and helping the Nasdaq 100 recover from its worst weekly decline since April’s tariff turmoil. However, about 65% of stocks in the S&P 500 still declined, indicating the rebound lacked broad-based support. “This rally was primarily driven by technology stocks rather than a broad return to risk appetite,” wrote Dilin Wu, strategist at Pepperstone Group Ltd., in a report.
At the Asian corporate level, Bloomberg data shows that SoftBank Group Corp.'s credit default swap (CDS) spread has risen to its highest level in nearly four years, reflecting growing market concerns over its AI-related financing and potential large-scale acquisitions.
Asian and U.S. stocks are showing divergent trends.
Underpinned by a technical rebound in U.S. equities, Asian markets failed to sustain gains on Monday, reflecting deeper investor skepticism about the prospects for AI-driven trading. The Nikkei 225 closed down 1.3% at 64,075.42, while the TOPIX fell 1.4% to 4,009.21.
Kazuyuki Muramatsu, Head of Investment Management at Nagomi Capital, noted that Elice’s sharp decline upon listing “indicates that the market environment for emerging cloud companies has not yet fully improved,” weighing on overall sentiment. He also emphasized that whether the market can truly stabilize will need to be verified by the upcoming earnings reports.
Bloomberg strategist Mark Cranfield also noted that the divergent performance among Asian assets has unsettled macro investors, further raising market expectations for the U.S. earnings season, particularly for tech giants.
The dollar weakened as the market awaited earnings results.
The U.S. dollar declined against all G10 currencies. Carol Kong, strategist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia, noted that investors are reluctant to take large positions ahead of the tech giants' earnings reports. “Risk sentiment and global growth prospects are now deeply tied to AI trading; investors are likely waiting to reassess their dollar positions after the earnings results are released.”
Meanwhile, U.S. Treasury yields, which rose on Monday due to reduced safe-haven demand, eased on Tuesday. Gold fell 0.5% to around $4,120 per ounce. Brent crude rose above $110.20 per barrel, as rising risks of further Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz countered overall stable oil flows in the Persian Gulf.
Political instability in France is putting pressure on the euro.
The euro's movement is also closely watched by the market. Protests over the cost of living in France escalated into violent clashes over the weekend, leading to widespread destruction and looting, prompting authorities to bolster security measures and pledge support to affected businesses. However, the French government carries a heavy debt burden and has one of the largest budget deficits in the eurozone, leaving it with extremely limited fiscal space to resolve social tensions through significant spending increases.
Thomas Hempell, Head of Macroeconomic and Market Research at Generali Investments, wrote in the report: "There are currently very few long positions on the euro. With the ongoing conflict in Iran and the unresolved political situation in France, a short-term rebound in the euro is unlikely."

articles.title: Jio IPO GMP Rises To 22% As India’s Biggest-Ever IPO Opens On October 21 - Outlook Money
articles.summary: Jio IPO GMP Rises To 22% As India’s Biggest-Ever IPO Opens On October 21  Outlook Money
articles.full_text:
- Jio Platforms IPO opens on October 21 and closes on October 23
- Latest GMP suggests a premium of about 22 per cent
- Jio IPO’s anchor book attracted Rs 2.5 lakh crore in bids
Jio Platforms’ initial public offering (IPO) is set to open for subscription on October 21. The issue will close on October 23. The Rs 30,213-crore IPO comprises a fresh issue of 270 million shares. It is set to be India’s largest-ever public issue, valuing Jio Platforms at around Rs 10.30 lakh crore at the upper end of the price band.
The price band is Rs 1,065-1,119 per share, and the lot size is 12 shares. Retail investors will need at least Rs 13,428 to apply at the upper price band. The allotment is expected to be finalised on October 26, and the shares are scheduled to list on the BSE and NSE on October 28.
As of October 20, Jio Platforms’ GMP stood at Rs 243 per share, indicating a potential listing price of Rs 1,362, or a 21.72 per cent premium over the upper price band of Rs 1,119. However, GMP is an unofficial indicator and can change before listing. The actual listing price may differ, and the premium does not guarantee listing gains.
Jio Platforms operates across mobile and fixed broadband connectivity, digital applications, enterprise services, cloud and artificial intelligence. Its subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm, had 533.3 million customers as of June 30, 2026.
Jio Platforms raised Rs 8,109.85 crore from 212 anchor investors on October 19, allotting 72.47 million shares at Rs 1,119 apiece. The anchor book received bids worth more than Rs 2.5 lakh crore, over 30 times the amount available for allocation.
The Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC) received the largest allocation, worth Rs 499.98 crore, accounting for 6.17 per cent of the anchor book. New World Fund Inc. received shares worth Rs 486.27 crore, or about 6 per cent, while the Government of Singapore was allotted shares worth Rs 340.93 crore, accounting for around 4.20 per cent.
SBI Focused Fund received an allocation worth Rs 315 crore, or about 3.88 per cent of the anchor book. BNP Paribas Financial Markets - ODI was allotted shares worth Rs 303.25 crore, accounting for around 3.74 per cent.
The anchor book also included global investment firms such as BlackRock, Fidelity Investments, Capital Group, T. Rowe Price, Schroders, JPMorgan Asset Management, Franklin Templeton and Invesco. Sovereign investors included the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, GIC, the Qatar Investment Authority and Norway’s sovereign wealth fund.
Domestic mutual funds received 34.34 per cent of the anchor allocation, worth Rs 2,784.96 crore. Life insurers and pension funds received 13.44 per cent, or Rs 1,089.95 crore. The remaining allocation went to other domestic and overseas institutional investors.
Jio Platforms plans to use Rs 27,500 crore from the issue proceeds to repay or prepay borrowings of its material subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm Ltd. The balance will be used for general corporate purposes.
The Jio IPO is entirely a fresh issue, meaning the company will issue new shares rather than existing shareholders selling their holdings through an offer for sale. Eligible Reliance Industries shareholders have a reserved portion worth up to Rs 2,500 crore, while employees have a reservation of up to 4.69 million shares and a discount of Rs 54 per share to the issue price.
Kotak Mahindra Capital Company is the book-running lead manager, and KFin Technologies is the registrar to the issue.
Jio Platforms reported total income of Rs 1,49,759.1 crore in FY26, up from Rs 1,29,333 crore in FY25 and Rs 1,10,175.4 crore in FY24.
Net profit rose to Rs 30,052.7 crore in FY26 from Rs 26,120.3 crore in FY25 and Rs 21,434 crore in FY24. Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) increased to Rs 76,255.4 crore in FY26, compared with Rs 64,170 crore in FY25 and Rs 54,958.7 crore in FY24.
For the June 2026 quarter, Jio Platforms reported total income of Rs 40,197.9 crore, net profit of Rs 7,764.1 crore and Ebitda of Rs 20,864.5 crore.
Its total debt stood at Rs 61,372.20 crore as of June 30, 2026, down from Rs 70,781 crore in the March quarter.

articles.title: 10-year Treasury yield moves lower after weak housing data - CNBC
articles.summary: 10-year Treasury yield moves lower after weak housing data  CNBC
articles.full_text:
The 10-year Treasury note yield fell on Tuesday as investors digested more economic data and continued to assess the inflationary backdrop ahead of the Federal Reserve’s interest rate decision next week.
The benchmark yield was down more than 2 basis points at 5.115%, while the 30-year Treasury bond fell more than 4 basis points to 5.426%. Meanwhile, the 2-year Treasury note yield was up more than 2 basis points at 4.785%.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Yields initially moved lower after housing starts for September missed expectations, coming in at 1.22 million versus the 1.3 million that economists polled by Dow Jones called for. September’s reading marked a 5.2% decrease from August’s revised estimate.
“The weakness in housing starts is not surprising given the surveys showing deep pessimism on the part of homebuilders given the shortage of labor from Washington’s immigration policies and the geopolitical risks kicking up inflation and the cost of building materials,” said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS. “It is not winter yet but housing is going into a deep freeze.”
Investors are awaiting other economic data releases this week, including Thursday’s release of weekly initial jobless claims.
This comes ahead of the Federal Reserve’s next interest rate decision, due next week. The latest figures for the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, the personal consumption expenditures index, will also be released next week.
Traders are now pricing in an 82% chance of the Fed holding interest rates steady, according to the CME FedWatch Tool. That’s up from 42.4% a month ago.
Concerns surrounding inflation have been exacerbated by a rise in crude oil prices following the start of the conflict in the Middle East earlier this year. On Tuesday, however, oil pulled back slightly, with West Texas Intermediate crude futures shedding 1.8% to close at $101.79 per barrel and Brent crude futures declining 0.69% to $108.79.

articles.title: Jio IPO Anchor Book: India Domestic Funds Took Nearly Half; Sovereign Wealth Validated $108 Billion - Tech Times
articles.summary: Jio IPO Anchor Book: India Domestic Funds Took Nearly Half; Sovereign Wealth Validated $108 Billion  Tech Times
articles.full_text:
Jio Platforms Limited closed its anchor investor allocation on Monday with a result that tells two distinct stories simultaneously: 212 of the world's most sophisticated institutional investors submitted bids exceeding Rs 2.5 lakh crore (approximately $26.3 billion) for just Rs 8,109.84 crore ($854 million) of available shares, an oversubscription ratio above 30 times that bankers close to the deal described as the strongest anchor-round demand ever recorded for an Indian mega-IPO.
The first story is the global one: sovereign wealth funds from Singapore, Abu Dhabi, and Norway joined the book alongside BlackRock, Fidelity, and Goldman Sachs, validating a $108 billion valuation in front of every major financial center on earth. The second story is less obvious but arguably more significant: nearly half the allocation — 47.78% — went to domestic Indian institutions, a proportion that would have been unthinkable for an issuance of this scale a generation ago.
The public subscription window for the Jio Platforms IPO is scheduled to open Wednesday, October 21, through Thursday, October 23, with a minimum retail lot of 12 shares at Rs 1,119 (~$11.78 per share), or approximately Rs 13,428 (~$141) at the upper end of the price band.
Anchor Book: Who's In
All 7.24 crore equity shares in the anchor tranche were allotted at Rs 1,119 — the upper end of the Rs 1,065–Rs 1,119 price band — confirming unanimous institutional consensus on the ceiling price.
Life Insurance Corporation of India secured the largest single allocation, with approximately Rs 500 crore of anchor shares (~$53 million), making the state-owned insurer the anchor of India's largest-ever anchor round. Sovereign wealth funds from three continents joined alongside it: Singapore's Government Investment Corporation received allocations worth approximately Rs 341 crore (~$36 million); the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA), which has held a direct stake in Jio Platforms since a 2020 pre-IPO investment round, deepened its exposure through the anchor tranche; and Norway's Government Pension Fund Global — the world's largest sovereign wealth fund by assets — also participated.
Global asset managers completed the international contingent. BlackRock, Fidelity, Amundi, Goldman Sachs, Schroders (approximately Rs 293 crore, ~$31 million), JP Morgan-managed funds (approximately Rs 182 crore, ~$19 million), Allianz Global, New World Fund, and Smallcap World Fund were among the 212 international anchor allocatees.
On the domestic side, SBI Mutual Fund, ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund, HDFC Mutual Fund, Kotak Mahindra Mutual Fund, Franklin Templeton, and Mirae Asset received allocations representing a combined 34.34% of the total anchor tranche — approximately 2.48 crore shares worth Rs 2,785 crore (~$293 million). Life insurers and pension funds — including SBI Life and HDFC Life — contributed an additional 13.44% of the tranche, approximately 97.4 lakh shares worth Rs 1,090 crore (~$115 million).
What Does Domestic Dominance Signal?
The 47.78% domestic institution share in the Jio Platforms anchor book is not merely a round-number curiosity; it represents a structural development in Indian capital markets that the final allocation data makes legible for the first time.
For comparison: when Hyundai Motor India completed its Rs 27,870 crore (~$2.93 billion) IPO in October 2024 — then India's largest — the domestic institution anchor share was substantially lower, with the book relying far more heavily on foreign institutional capital for its initial price validation. When LIC itself listed in May 2022, its Rs 21,000 crore (~$2.21 billion at current rates) offering, while anchored in part by state-aligned domestic investors, did not produce an anchor book in which private domestic institutions held nearly half the allocation independently.
A generation ago, Indian companies seeking to raise capital at this scale would have designed their pre-IPO investor rosters primarily around foreign institutional validation — the Singapore sovereign fund, the Abu Dhabi fund, the American asset manager — because the domestic institutional ecosystem was not deep enough to absorb this proportion of a record-breaking issuance. The domestic mutual fund industry has grown approximately tenfold in the past decade, reaching Rs 70+ lakh crore in combined assets under management by mid-2026. The result visible in Monday's anchor book is that the capital Jio Platforms needs to list successfully no longer has to be sourced primarily from abroad — India's own institutions, responding to the savings and investment behavior of hundreds of millions of Indian households, can now anchor what would have required heavy foreign dependency a decade earlier.
That matters for post-listing price dynamics. Domestic mutual funds and insurance companies in India operate under SEBI and IRDAI mandates that constrain short-term trading; their average holding period for large-cap equity positions is typically measured in years, not quarters. A 47.78% anchor tranche held by domestic long-duration investors creates structural price support during the anchor lock-in period — and likely well beyond — that a foreign-capital-dominant book cannot reliably provide.
Under SEBI's ICDR Regulations, anchor investors are subject to a two-tier lock-in: 50% of allocated shares are freed after 30 days (around November 27, 2026), with the remaining 50% locked until 90 days after allotment (approximately January 26, 2027). When the first tranche of anchor shares unlocks in late November, the selling pressure calculus will be very different from an anchor book where short-duration foreign capital represents the majority.
The composition also accelerates the mechanics of index inclusion. At a post-listing market capitalization of approximately $108 billion, Jio Platforms will be a strong candidate for inclusion in MSCI India, FTSE All-World, and eventually the Nifty 50. Each inclusion event triggers mandatory buying by passive ETFs and index-tracking funds globally — estimated at $500 million to $2 billion per MSCI event for a company of this size. The domestic institution anchor share, by holding a substantial portion of available equity in patient hands, constrains the float available to passive buyers during the inclusion rebalancing window, potentially amplifying the price response to each inclusion.
The Offering at a Glance
| Detail | Value | 
|---|---|
| Price Band | Rs 1,065–Rs 1,119 per share (~$11.21–$11.78) | 
| Fresh Issue Size | Up to 27 crore equity shares | 
| Total IPO Size | ~Rs 30,213 crore (~$3.18 billion) | 
| Implied Valuation | ~Rs 10.3 lakh crore (~$108 billion) | 
| Lot Size | 12 shares | 
| Employee Discount | Rs 54 per share (~$0.57) | 
| Employee Reservation | Rs 500 crore (~$53 million) | 
| Shareholder Reservation | Rs 2,500 crore (~$263 million) | 
| Public Subscription | October 21–23, 2026 | 
| Allotment | October 26, 2026 | 
| Listing (BSE & NSE) | October 28, 2026 | 
The Jio Platforms IPO carries no Offer for Sale component. None of the company's existing institutional shareholders — including Meta Platforms, Alphabet, KKR, Vista Equity Partners, Silver Lake, Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, ADIA, and Mubadala — are liquidating any shares at this stage. Every rupee of proceeds flows directly to the company.
How Does an Anchor Investor Allocation Work?
The anchor investor mechanism is a SEBI-designed tool that serves a specific market function: it allows the most-resourced institutional investors to receive priority allocation one business day before the public subscription opens, in exchange for a two-tier lock-in on their shares — 50% freed after 30 days, the remaining 50% after 90 days.
Under SEBI's Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements (ICDR) Regulations, up to 60% of the Qualified Institutional Buyer (QIB) tranche — typically 75% of the total net offer — can be allocated to anchor investors. Applications must be a minimum of Rs 10 crore per institution. The allocation price is set at the upper end of the price band — in this case, Rs 1,119 — which simultaneously disciplines anchor investors (they are committing at the highest possible entry price) and signals to all subsequent investors that the most analytically sophisticated buyers assessed fair value at the ceiling.
The 30x oversubscription ratio — more than Rs 2.5 lakh crore in bids for Rs 8,110 crore of available allocation — is the result of a structural ceiling: only 60% of the QIB tranche is available to anchor investors, regardless of how many institutions apply. Hundreds of eligible QIBs submitted applications that could not be accommodated. The allocation committee, working with the lead managers, allocated shares with preference given to institutions demonstrating long-term holding mandates — which explains why domestic life insurers and pension funds received proportionally significant allocations alongside, or in preference to, short-duration foreign hedge funds.
What Monday's anchor session produced, mechanically, is a price signal that retail investors and HNIs cannot ignore: 212 institutions, each required to apply for a minimum of Rs 10 crore and each subject to a lock-in (50% for 30 days, 50% for 90 days), simultaneously concluded that Rs 1,119 was not only acceptable but worth competing for at 30x oversubscription. That is the strongest form of institutional price validation the Indian regulatory framework permits before a retail subscription window opens.
For retail investors considering whether to apply during the October 21–23 window, the anchor mechanism provides one piece of actionable data: the price discovery process has already concluded in favor of the upper band, and the most informed participants in that process have accepted a multi-month lock-in to say so.
Where the Money Goes
The Red Herring Prospectus earmarks up to Rs 27,500 crore of gross proceeds (~$2.89 billion) for prepayment of borrowings at Relia

articles.title: Jio IPO anchor book draws record Rs 2.5 lakh crore demand; LIC, BlackRock, Capital Group lead allocations - Mathrubhumi English
articles.summary: Jio IPO anchor book draws record Rs 2.5 lakh crore demand; LIC, BlackRock, Capital Group lead allocations  Mathrubhumi English
articles.full_text:
Mumbai: Jio Platforms Ltd has set an unprecedented benchmark in India's primary equity market, attracting institutional demand of more than Rs 2.5 lakh crore for its Rs 8,110-crore anchor book -- an oversubscription of over 30 times. The allocation, finalised at Rs 1,119 a share, drew more than 200 investor lines from global asset managers, sovereign wealth funds, pension funds, insurers, mutual funds, hedge funds and Indian family offices.
The company allotted 7,24,74,066 equity shares to anchor investors, raising Rs 8,109.85 crore ahead of the IPO’s public subscription opening on October 21. Banking sources said the aggregate institutional demand was the first time an Indian IPO anchor book had crossed the Rs 2.5-lakh-crore mark.
Also Read: Jio's ₹30,000-crore IPO is a referendum on who pays for India's digital infrastructure
For the uninitiated, an anchor book is the portion of an IPO reserved for large institutional investors -- such as mutual funds, insurers, pension funds, sovereign wealth funds and global asset managers -- who are allotted shares before the public subscription opens. Their early commitments are meant to signal confidence in the issue and provide a stable base of long-term capital.
A record institutional response
The anchor book included global asset managers, sovereign wealth funds, pension funds, insurers, domestic mutual funds, technology-focused investors, alternative asset managers and family offices. Jio Platforms is a subsidiary of Reliance Industries and its IPO is expected to be among India’s largest public offerings.
Also Read: Jio IPO: Rs 30,213-crore bet on India’s digital future: 10 things investors must know
Life Insurance Corporation of India received the largest single allocation in the entire anchor book: 44,68,128 shares worth nearly Rs 500 crore, or 6.17% of the anchor portion.
India's largest mutual funds also secured prominent allocations. SBI Mutual Fund, ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund and HDFC Mutual Fund each received Rs 425 crore, while Aditya Birla Sun Life Mutual Fund received Rs 300 crore. Kotak Mutual Fund and Nippon India Mutual Fund were allocated Rs 200 crore each.
Domestic insurers and pension institutions added further depth. HDFC Life and SBI Life received Rs 100 crore each, while SBI Pension/NPS Trust and HDFC Pension received Rs 100 crore each. ICICI Prudential Pension, UTI Pension and several life and general insurers also participated.
Global managers take large positions
The international tranche featured some of the world's largest asset managers. BlackRock, Capital International and Fidelity Management & Research (FMR) each received Rs 425 crore, while Singapore sovereign investor GIC also secured Rs 425 crore.
Also Read: Jio Platforms IPO opens October 21: Price band, lot size, employee discount and key dates
Capital Group’s participation extended across two vehicles: Capital International at Rs 425 crore and Capital World at Rs 300 crore. FMR received Rs 425 crore, with its international affiliate FIL taking a separate Rs 50-crore allocation. Fidelity Contra Fund, among the largest active global mutual funds, was reported to be among the top individual anchor allocators.
Schroders received Rs 293 crore, JPMorgan Asset Management Rs 182 crore and Allianz Rs 150 crore. Technology-focused managers Ninety One and Dragoneer received Rs 200 crore and Rs 150 crore respectively, while Janus Henderson took Rs 50 crore.
Sovereign wealth funds also featured prominently. Besides GIC, the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority and Qatar Investment Authority received Rs 150 crore each, while Norway’s Norges Bank was allocated Rs 50 crore. Global pension commitments came from Canada’s PSP Investments, CalSTRS and the Florida Retirement System.
High-profile global investors
BlackRock is the world's largest asset manager, overseeing trillions of dollars in client assets across index funds, exchange-traded funds, active strategies and alternatives. Its Rs 425-crore allocation signals interest from one of the most influential global owners of public equities.
Capital Group is a major US active investment manager known for long-term, research-driven equity investing. Its flagship global vehicles include the New World Fund, which received an allocation of Rs 486.2 crore; Capital International and Capital World also received separate allocations of Rs 425 crore and Rs 300 crore respectively.
FMR/Fidelity Investments is the investment-management arm of Fidelity Investments and one of the largest active managers globally. FMR secured Rs 425 crore, while FIL, its international affiliate, received Rs 50 crore. Fidelity Contra Fund, a major US active mutual fund, was among the leading individual anchor allocators.
Schroders is a UK-headquartered global asset manager with a strong presence in active equity, fixed income, multi-asset and alternatives. Its Rs 293-crore allocation makes it one of the larger international participants in the Jio anchor book.
JPMorgan Asset Management is the asset-management arm of JPMorgan Chase, managing global equity, fixed-income, multi-asset and alternative strategies. It received Rs 182 crore in the anchor allocation.
Ninety One is a global active asset manager with particular strength in emerging-market and technology-oriented strategies. Its Rs 200-crore allocation underscores the appeal of Jio’s digital-infrastructure and telecom platform among specialist growth investors.
Dragoneer is a US-based growth investor focused on technology and internet companies. Its Rs 150-crore allocation reflects demand from investors that typically back high-growth digital businesses.
Janus Henderson is a global active asset manager formed through the merger of Janus Capital and Henderson Global Investors. It received Rs 50 crore and was among the specialist global managers participating in the book.
Sovereign and pension capital
The presence of GIC, ADIA, QIA and Norges Bank highlights the role of sovereign wealth funds in India’s largest new listings. These investors generally pursue long-duration positions and can provide stability to the post-listing shareholder base.
Also Read: Jio’s first decade: 524 million users, 240 EB data and a home-grown 6G blueprint
Pension managers, including PSP Investments, CalSTRS and the Florida Retirement System, also participated. Their involvement reinforces the positioning of Jio Platforms as a long-term infrastructure and digital-services holding rather than a purely speculative technology listing.
Alternative capital and family offices
Alternative and multi-strategy investors also secured allocations. 360 One Asset Management received Rs 100 crore, while Blackstone, Citadel Securities, Marshall Wace and Millennium received Rs 50 crore each. Balyasny, MK Ventures and Value Partners were allocated Rs 10 crore each.
Indian family offices and private-wealth vehicles added a domestic high-net-worth dimension. Enam Family Office, Premji Invest and HCL Family Office received Rs 50 crore each, while Rainmatter/Zerodha Family Office received Rs 25 crore.
What the demand signals
The record anchor response is being read as a strong institutional endorsement of Jio Platforms’ scale, cash flows and position in India’s digital economy. It also reflects the depth of global capital available for large Indian listings at a time when foreign and domestic institutions are seeking exposure to the country’s telecom, data and digital-services growth.
For the issuer, the anchor allocation provides a high-quality institutional base before the retail and non-institutional portions open. For the market, the more than 30-times oversubscription and 200-plus investor lines set a new reference point for demand in India’s IPO ecosystem.
The public issue opens on October 21. The anchor book’s final demand figure will remain subject to the usual regulatory disclosures, but banking sources described the response as the largest ever for an Indian IPO anchor allocation.
