articles.summary: GCash IPO Breaks Records, Elevates Philippine Fintech to Global Spotlight  Daily Tribune
articles.full_text:
GCash parent Mynt Inc. has put the Philippines back in the spotlight of global investors after pulling off Southeast Asia’s biggest initial public offering (IPO) since 2021, defying weak market conditions and drawing strong international demand.
J.P. Morgan, which served as joint global coordinator and joint bookrunner, said the landmark offering was valued at up to P60.9 billion, or $970 million, assuming the full exercise of the overallotment option.
The transaction was also ASEAN’s largest technology, media and telecommunications IPO since 2021 amid the growing appeal of local digital businesses to international investors.
Mynt officially debuted on the Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE) under the ticker symbol GCASH, with its shares priced at P6.60 apiece.
“This is a significant milestone for the Philippines. It demonstrates that a high-quality Philippine digital business can attract strong global and domestic investor support while expanding investment opportunities in the country,” J.P. Morgan Philippines Senior Country Officer Carlos Ma. G. Mendoza said.
“As the largest IPO in Philippine history, this deal also marks an important step in the continued development of Philippine capital markets. We are proud to have led this landmark IPO and to continue supporting Mynt, Inc. across our banking franchise,” he added.
J.P. Morgan said nearly 200 institutional investors across Asia, Europe and the United States were engaged throughout the marketing process.
The order book was multiple times oversubscribed, attracting global long-only investors, sovereign wealth funds, domestic institutions and multi-strategy funds.
Strong demand came despite subdued market liquidity and challenging market conditions, boosting the Philippine equities market as it seeks to attract more major listings.
PSE President and CEO Ramon Monzon said Mynt entered the exchange with a market capitalization of P441.5 billion, or approximately $7 billion, making it the seventh-largest domestic listed company based on the previous day’s closing prices.
Monzon said 19 foreign and six domestic cornerstone investors subscribed to 59.8 percent of the offered shares, while non-cornerstone institutional investors accounted for another 21.9 percent.
Local trading participants also submitted orders for more than 2.65 billion shares against an allocation of 1.6 billion shares, equivalent to 165.5 percent of the allocation.
Retail participation was equally significant, with 140,725 GCash subscribers investing approximately P1.1 billion through the application.
Monzon described the listing as the culmination of a three-year effort to bring one of the country’s leading fintech companies to the exchange.
Mynt President and CEO Martha Sazon, meanwhile, said the company remains focused on extending financial services to Filipinos who continue to face barriers to traditional banking.
“Becoming a public company is not the finish line. The opportunity ahead is about how much more we can make possible for every Filipino,” Sazon said.
“It opens up more ways for us to reach those who are still unbanked and underserved,” she added.
Sazon said nearly 90 percent of GCash customers come from low- and middle-income households, reflecting the company’s focus on financial inclusion.

articles.title: Jio IPO draws global investors despite FPI selling in Indian equities - Who invested? - ET Now
articles.summary: Jio IPO draws global investors despite FPI selling in Indian equities - Who invested?  ET Now
articles.full_text:
Jio Platforms IPO: Even as foreign investors continue to withdraw money from Indian equities, some of the world's biggest investment institutions have participated in Mukesh Ambani-led Jio Platforms' initial public offering, highlighting a contrast between broader market outflows and demand for the upcoming public issue. 
Global investment firms, including BlackRock, Fidelity, Capital Group, Schroders and JPMorgan Asset Management, feature among the anchor investors in Jio Platforms' Rs 30,213 crore IPO, which opens for public subscription on Wednesday, October 21. 
The company has allotted shares worth Rs 8,109.85 crore to 212 anchor investors at Rs 1,119 per share, the upper end of its IPO price band, according to a stock exchange filing. 
The anchor book attracted institutional demand exceeding Rs 2.5 lakh crore, more than 30 times the available allocation.
FPIs sell Indian equities, but global investors participate in Jio IPO 
Foreign portfolio investors have remained net sellers in Indian equities amid volatility in domestic and global markets. 
According to market reports, FPIs had withdrawn around Rs 52,100 crore from Indian equities in October 2026 through October 19, taking their reported outflows for the calendar year to approximately Rs 3.12 lakh crore. 
Against this backdrop, participation by major overseas investment institutions in the Jio IPO presents an interesting contrast. 
However, the two figures are not directly comparable. FPI outflows represent net selling across Indian equities, while the Jio anchor book includes allocations to both domestic and overseas institutions.
The participation of overseas investors in the IPO also does not necessarily mean that the same institutions have been selling shares in the secondary market. 
Jio IPO: Which global investors received shares?
According to the anchor allocation filing, several major global investment institutions participated in the offering. 
New World Fund Inc, associated with Capital Group, received shares worth Rs 486.27 crore, making it one of the largest anchor investors. 
The Government of Singapore was allotted shares worth Rs 340.93 crore, while the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority received an allocation worth approximately Rs 150 crore. 
Other global investment institutions represented in the anchor book included BlackRock, Fidelity, Schroders, JPMorgan Asset Management, T. Rowe Price and Allianz Global Investors.
The anchor book also attracted participation from several international investment funds with exposure to technology and emerging-market businesses. 
Jio IPO: Sovereign wealth funds also participate 
Apart from global asset managers, the Jio IPO attracted interest from sovereign wealth funds and other long-term institutional investors. 
The Government of Singapore and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority were among the major overseas institutions receiving anchor allocations. 
Their participation comes as Jio Platforms prepares for one of the largest public market listings in Indian corporate history. 
Jio IPO: Domestic institutions receive nearly half the anchor book 
While overseas investors participated in the offering, domestic mutual funds, life insurers and pension funds also received substantial allocations.
Domestic mutual funds were allotted 2.489 crore shares worth Rs 2,784.96 crore, representing 34.34 per cent of the anchor book. 
Life insurance companies and pension funds received 97.4 lakh shares worth Rs 1,089.95 crore, accounting for another 13.44 per cent. 
Together, these categories received shares worth approximately Rs 3,874.91 crore, or 47.78 per cent of the total anchor allocation. 
The remaining anchor allocation includes overseas investors as well as other domestic institutions. The exchange filing does not separately provide a consolidated figure for total FPI participation. 
Why is Jio IPO attracting global investors? 
Jio Platforms operates one of the world's largest mobile networks by subscriber numbers and has expanded into broadband, digital entertainment, cloud computing and enterprise services. 
As of June 2026, the company had 533.3 million subscribers and carried nearly 60 per cent of India's data traffic, according to reported company figures. 
The IPO will give public-market investors direct exposure to Jio Platforms, which has so far operated as a subsidiary of Reliance Industries. 
The company's subscriber base, digital services businesses and growth opportunities provide important factors for investors to assess. 
However, individual overseas institutions have not publicly disclosed their reasons for participating in the anchor book. 
What does the contrast between FPI selling and Jio IPO demand indicate? 
Foreign investors can reduce their overall exposure to Indian equities while continuing to invest in selected companies or new public offerings. 
Selling in the secondary market and participating in an IPO are different investment decisions. They can also involve different funds and institutions. 
The participation of global investment institutions in Jio's anchor book therefore shows interest in this particular offering, but does not necessarily indicate a reversal in broader FPI selling. 
The response to the public issue will provide a clearer indication of demand from retail investors and other market participants. 
Jio IPO price band, issue size and subscription dates
Jio Platforms plans to raise approximately Rs 30,213 crore through a fresh issue of up to 27 crore equity shares. The IPO price band has been fixed at Rs 1,065 to Rs 1,119 per share. 
The public issue will open on October 21 and close on October 23. 
According to the offer documents, the offering values Jio Platforms at approximately USD 108 billion. 
Part of the proceeds will be used to repay debt at its telecom subsidiary, while the remaining funds will be used for general corporate purposes. 
Reliance Industries will continue to hold a majority stake in Jio Platforms after the listing.

articles.title: IPO Rulebook Set for a Clean-Up? SEBI’s New Panel Could Make Going Public Easier - NiftyTrader
articles.summary: IPO Rulebook Set for a Clean-Up? SEBI’s New Panel Could Make Going Public Easier  NiftyTrader
articles.full_text:
SEBI Moves to Review IPO Rulebook as Capital Market Reforms Gather Pace
India’s capital market regulator is preparing to review the rules that govern how companies raise money from investors. The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has formed a working group to examine regulations covering initial public offerings (IPOs), follow-on public offerings (FPOs) and other securities issuances, according to sources cited by Moneycontrol.
The move could bring changes to the regulatory framework used by companies entering the stock market or raising additional capital. For investors tracking upcoming IPOs, the key question is whether the proposed review will improve transparency and make the fundraising process more efficient.
Track Live : IPO – Latest & Upcoming IPOs List 2026 | Check Live BSE NSE IPOs
IPO Rulebook : SEBI Working Group Will Examine IPO and FPO Regulations
The working group will review SEBI’s Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements (ICDR) Regulations, which establish the rules companies must follow when raising capital.
The review will cover several fundraising routes, including IPOs, FPOs, preferential issues and rights issues. These regulations govern important aspects of public offerings, from eligibility and disclosures to pricing, allotment and procedural requirements.
According to industry sources, the group will focus on simplifying regulatory requirements, removing overlapping provisions and refining the language of the existing rules.
The objective is to make SEBI IPO regulations clearer and more efficient without losing sight of investor protection.
What exactly has SEBI announced?
- Regulations under review: SEBI has initiated a review of its Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements (ICDR) Regulations, 2018, which govern IPOs, FPOs, preferential issues, rights issues and other specified methods of raising capital.
- Main objective: The review aims to simplify regulatory requirements, remove duplicate provisions, clarify legal language and make the capital-raising framework more efficient for companies and market intermediaries.
- Review mechanism: A working group is being formed under SEBI’s Primary Markets Advisory Committee (PMAC), which advises the regulator on primary-market matters. SEBI said the decision to constitute the working group was taken at a PMAC meeting on August 12, 2026.
- Scope of the review: The group will examine relevant ICDR provisions to identify areas that may require clarification, rationalisation, modification or simplification.
- Current status: The review process has been initiated, but the reported exercise has not yet resulted in confirmed final amendments. Any proposed changes will need to follow the applicable SEBI regulatory process before implementation.
Why SEBI Wants to Simplify the Existing Regulatory Framework
Complex or overlapping regulations can increase compliance work for companies and market intermediaries. A clearer framework could help issuers understand their obligations and navigate the fundraising process more efficiently.
SEBI Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey had earlier indicated that the regulator would review both the ICDR Regulations and the SEBI Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements (LODR) Regulations.
While ICDR rules focus on raising capital, LODR regulations govern the disclosure and compliance obligations of listed companies. Reviewing both frameworks reflects SEBI’s broader effort to streamline capital market regulations.
However, the working group’s formation does not mean that any specific rule changes have been finalised. The impact will depend on the recommendations and any subsequent regulatory decisions.
Track Live : Nifty Levels Today | Sensex Levels Today
What do IPO, FPO, preferential issue and rights issue mean?
Companies use different methods to raise money from investors. According to SEBI’s investor guidance, these methods differ mainly in whether the company is unlisted or already listed and who is eligible to receive the shares.
1. IPO — Initial Public Offering
- Meaning: An unlisted company offers shares to the public for the first time.
- Purpose: To raise capital for expansion, business operations, debt repayment or other corporate needs. An IPO can also include existing shareholders selling their shares.
- Example: A growing company offers shares to public investors and lists on a stock exchange.
- Key point: An IPO provides a route for a company to become publicly listed.
2. FPO — Follow-on Public Offering
- Meaning: An already-listed company offers shares to the public through a further public offering.
- Purpose: To raise additional capital after its initial listing or allow existing shareholders to sell shares through an offer for sale.
- Example: A listed company issues additional shares to fund a new factory or reduce its debt.
- Key point: Unlike an IPO, an FPO is conducted by a company that is already listed.
3. Preferential Issue
- Meaning: A listed company issues securities to selected investors or a specified group of persons through a private-placement route, subject to applicable SEBI regulations.
- Purpose: To raise capital from identified investors rather than through a general public offer.
- Example: A listed company issues new shares to a particular institutional investor to finance its expansion.
- Key point: The offer is directed to selected investors, not the general public.
4. Rights Issue
- Meaning: A company offers additional shares to its existing eligible shareholders, based on a specified record date and the terms of the issue.
- Purpose: To raise funds while giving existing shareholders an opportunity to purchase additional shares.
- Example: A company offers one additional share for every five shares held by an eligible shareholder.
- Key point: Eligible existing shareholders receive the opportunity to subscribe, generally in proportion to their current holdings.
Key differences at a glance
| Feature | IPO | FPO | Preferential issue | Rights issue | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Company status | Unlisted | Already listed | Generally listed under SEBI ICDR rules | Listed issuer under SEBI ICDR rules | 
| Who receives the offer? | Public investors | Public investors | Selected investors | Existing eligible shareholders | 
| Main purpose | Initial public offering and listing | Further public fundraising | Targeted fundraising | Fundraising from existing shareholders | 
| Is it a public offer? | Yes | Yes | No, it is a private-placement route | No, it is offered to eligible existing shareholders | 
Source: SEBI’s ICDR guidance and investor education materials.
SEBI’s Other Proposals Could Also Affect the IPO Market
The latest review comes alongside other regulatory initiatives concerning public fundraising.
SEBI has floated a consultation paper proposing changes to the monitoring of funds raised through public issues. The aim is to review the framework for overseeing how companies use money collected from investors.
Separately, the regulator has proposed changes to the rules governing small and medium enterprise (SME) IPOs, including a review of eligibility criteria and other requirements.
Together, these initiatives indicate that SEBI is examining several aspects of the capital-raising process, although each proposal remains subject to its own regulatory process.
What is the ICDR Regulations framework?
ICDR stands for Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements. SEBI introduced the 2018 regulations to establish requirements for companies issuing securities through public issues and other specified routes.
The framework covers several important areas:
| Regulatory area | What it governs | 
|---|---|
| Eligibility | Whether a company meets the applicable conditions to launch an issue | 
| Disclosure requirements | Information that must be provided to investors in offer documents | 
| Pricing | Rules and requirements relating to the pricing of securities | 
| Allotment | How securities are allocated to eligible investors under the applicable framework | 
| Promoters’ contribution and lock-in | Applicable contribution requirements and restrictions on selling certain holdings for specified periods | 
| Procedures and compliance | Filing, documentation and other obligations for issuers and intermediaries | 
What SEBI’s IPO Rule Review Means for Investors
For investors, the main issue is whether the review ultimately improves the quality of disclosures, strengthens accountability and makes IPO participation easier to evaluate.
A more efficient framework could support companies seeking capital and potentially improve the overall functioning of India’s primary market. Stronger clarity around fundraising and the use of proceeds could also help investors assess risks more effectively.
However, simplified rules do not automatically make every IPO attractive. Investors should continue to examine company financials, valuations, business prospects, risks and the intended use of funds before applying.
Read More : Adani Energy Solutions Q2 FY27 Results on Oct 22, Investor Call on Oct 23: What to Watch
Here’s What Happened Today and Why Traders Reacted
SEBI’s decision to review IPO and FPO regulations is a regulatory development rather than an immediate market-moving earnings announcement.
Investors may view the initiative positively if it eventually reduces unnecessary compliance burdens, improves disclosure standards and makes capital raising more predictable. Companies planning to list could benefit from greater regulatory clarity.
However, there is no confirmed evidence in the information available that the announcement alone has triggered a significant move in the broader stock market.
Traders should therefore distinguish between the potential long-term benefits of regulatory reform and immediate price movements driven by earnings, valuations, market liquidity or broader economic developments.

articles.full_text:
The IPO is priced at Rs 1,065-1,119 per share and will open on October 21, closing on October 23. At the upper end of the price band, the grey market premium points to an indicative listing price of Rs 1,364 per share.
The issue comprises 27 crore shares and is entirely a fresh issue, making it India’s largest public offer. Jio Platforms intends to use Rs 27,500 crore of the proceeds to repay or prepay borrowings. At the upper price band, the company’s post-issue market capitalisation is estimated at Rs 10.30 lakh crore.
Jio IPO raises Rs 8,110 from anchor investors
Mukesh Ambani-led Jio Platforms has raised nearly Rs 8,110 crore from 212 anchor investor accounts and schemes ahead of its Rs 30,213 crore initial public offering, which opens for public subscription on Wednesday. The investors include Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC), BlackRock, Fidelity, Singapore's sovereign wealth fund GIC and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority.
The telecom and digital services company allotted 7.25 crore shares to anchor investors at Rs 1,119 apiece, the upper end of its IPO price band, according to an exchange filing on Monday.
Among overseas investors, the Government of Singapore received 30.47 lakh shares worth nearly Rs 341 crore, while the Monetary Authority of Singapore was allotted shares worth Rs 84 crore. Abu Dhabi Investment Authority secured an allocation of about Rs 150 crore through its Monsoon investment vehicle.
Global asset managers BlackRock and Fidelity participated through multiple funds and investment accounts. Other investors in the anchor book included Allianz Global Investors, Ninety One, JPMorgan, Schroders, Capital Group, Florida Retirement System and California State Teachers' Retirement System.
The allocation also featured schemes managed by HDFC Mutual Fund, ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund, SBI Mutual Fund, Nippon India Mutual Fund, Kotak Mutual Fund, Axis Mutual Fund, Aditya Birla Sun Life Mutual Fund and Mirae Asset Mutual Fund. Insurance companies such as HDFC Life, SBI Life, ICICI Prudential Life, Axis Max Life and Kotak Mahindra Life were also among the allottees.
What are brokerages saying?
Emkay Global has recommended a ‘Subscribe’ rating to the IPO, highlighting Jio’s leading position in India’s telecom market and its growing footprint across broadband, enterprise connectivity and digital services.
Through Reliance Jio Infocomm, Jio Platforms operates the country’s largest telecom network. As of June 2026, it had 533.3 million customers, accounting for 50% of wireless broadband subscribers and 42.6% of fixed broadband subscribers. Its network carries around 60% of India’s wireless data traffic. According to Emkay, Jio also has the largest 5G customer base outside China.
Emkay expects Jio’s future growth to come from a broader range of businesses beyond mobile connectivity. The company plans to consolidate its position in mobility through greater 5G adoption and the migration of customers from 2G to 4G and 5G. Home broadband is another key growth area, while its relationships with enterprises and small businesses are expected to expand through managed services. Jio also plans to offer its proprietary technology stack to telecom operators overseas.
Its digital-services portfolio spans entertainment, cloud, gaming, smart-home solutions, the Internet of Things, communication and artificial intelligence-enabled platforms. These include MyJio, JioTV+, JioSaavn, JioGames, JioAICloud, JioPC and JioBrain. For enterprise customers, the company offers internet leased lines, MPLS, VPN, CPaaS, managed Wi-Fi, private 5G, SD-WAN, cloud, cybersecurity and managed network services.
Technology development is another part of Jio’s strategy. The company has built an integrated technology stack covering network infrastructure, device engineering, software, operating systems and digital applications. In the first quarter of FY27, it had 12,477 employees working on digital product and technology development, accounting for around 45% of its workforce. Its investments include research into 6G, cloud-native platforms, network automation and new digital services.
On valuation, Emkay places Jio Platforms at 31.7-33.3 times FY26 earnings and 15-15.6 times FY26 EBITDA at the upper end of the IPO price band. SBI Securities estimates a post-issue FY26 price-to-earnings multiple of 34.4 times at the same price and values the company at Rs 20,117 per subscriber on an enterprise value basis.
These valuations reflect Jio’s scale, earnings growth, technology capabilities and potential to monetise its businesses over the long term, according to the brokerage.
SBI Securities has also highlighted the company’s continuing capital expenditure needs, reliance on infrastructure providers, cybersecurity and privacy risks, dependence on spectrum licences and the possibility of network disruptions.
Jio Platforms IPO financials
The company’s cash generation and profitability have also improved. Jio Platforms reported operating cash flow of Rs 77,556 crore and free cash flow of Rs 43,301 crore in FY26. EBITDA increased from Rs 54,341 crore in FY24 to Rs 73,382 crore in FY26, while profit after tax rose from Rs 21,422 crore to Rs 30,064 crore. Its EBITDA margin edged up from 49.6% in FY24 to 50% in FY26.
Emkay expects cash generation to improve further as the 5G investment cycle approaches its end. The IPO note also states that repayment of borrowings by Reliance Jio Infocomm should reduce leverage and finance costs, support cash flows and provide greater financial flexibility for future investments.

articles.title: BMW Patents New Electric Scotoer In India - No Helmet, No Riding Gear, Self Balancing Tech - RushLane
articles.summary: BMW Patents New Electric Scotoer In India - No Helmet, No Riding Gear, Self Balancing Tech  RushLane
articles.full_text:
With the use of advanced tech, BMW Vision CE aims to make the two-wheeler experience much safer and more enjoyable
BMW Motorrad has come up with exciting designs for its electric two-wheelers, as evident from products like the CE 02 and CE 04. An even bolder product idea is currently under development, based on the BMW Vision CE concept showcased last year. While an official launch timeline has not been announced, the BMW Vision CE self-balancing electric two-wheeler has been patented in India.
Self-balancing, 360° rider protection
BMW Vision CE is entirely self-balancing and does not even require a stand to remain upright when stationary. This makes the overall experience quite similar to a car, as riders do not have to put their feet down when starting or coming to a halt. The self-balancing function is likely powered by an advanced system comprising sensors and electric actuators.
While the scooter is self-balancing, a stand is still provided. This will apparently be used when the scooter is turned off and parked for long periods. During this time, the self-balancing system disengages to conserve battery and avoid component strain. The self-balancing system is likely automatically activated when the scooter is turned on again.
Safety of the rider is another focus area for BMW Vision CE. With this electric scooter, riders don’t need to use protective gear such as a helmet, gloves and specialized clothing. A tubular steel frame has been used at the front, which is designed to protect the rider’s feet and legs. Protective gear is not needed, since the scooter has a robust cage all around. Moreover, BMW Vision CE has a four point seatbelt, which secures the rider to their seat.
This will protect the rider in case of a crash or tip-over. Side elements have been engineered into the frame structure to protect the hip and shoulder areas. Adequate foam cushioning has been provided on the cage, backrest, handlebar and other parts to minimize potential injuries during an impact. Vision CE is likely to be equipped with rear-facing radar and driver-assistance electronics to detect potential collisions before they occur.
Performance, range
Specifications of BMW Vision CE have not been revealed. However, speculative reports opine that the self-balancing scooter could be derived from the platform used for CE 04. The latter uses an 8.5 kWh high voltage battery pack, allowing a range of 130 km. Powered by a permanent magnet liquid cooled synchronous motor, the CE 04 delivers 42 hp of max power and 62 Nm of peak torque. Top speed is electrically limited to 120 km/h.
With the additional safety equipment used with BMW Vision CE, the scooter could be heavier. That could impact its range and top speed. However, changes in the battery pack and the electric motor could help achieve the desired performance. While a design patent has been filed, there is no clarity on the launch dates. BMW Vision CE has been patented in other markets as well, although production plans have not been announced.

Stock Market Holiday Today: Indian stock markets are closed on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, on account of Dussehra (Vijayadashami), one of the major Hindu festivals that symbolises the victory of good over evil. After the one-day holiday, trading on NSE and BSE will resume on Wednesday, October 21, with markets reopening from their previous closing levels recorded on Monday, October 19.

URBANA, Ill. (RFD-TV) — Farmers are expected to receive record 2025 Agriculture Risk Coverage and Price Loss Coverage payments by the end of October, according to a new farmdoc daily analysis from the University of Illinois.
Farmdoc estimates total payments across eligible commodities at just over $13.2 billion, compared with USDA’s publicized estimate of $13.8 billion. Corn, soybean and wheat payments account for more than $9 billion of the total.
Average payments are estimated at $51 per corn base acre, $29 per soybean acre, and $47 per wheat acre. Rice, peanuts and seed cotton carry some of the highest per-acre support rates.
The larger payments reflect lower 2025 commodity prices and program changes enacted in 2025. Producers also receive whichever is higher between ARC-County and PLC for 2025, regardless of their original enrollment choice.
That one-time provision ends for 2026. Enrollment is now open, and producers must again choose between ARC and PLC by December 11.

articles.summary: India VIX jumps over 6%; Nifty, Sensex fall 1.5% - Check key reasons why stock markets are falling today  ET Now
articles.full_text:
India’s volatility index, India VIX, jumped more than 6 per cent after the benchmark indices fell over 1.3 per cent in today's trade (October 19). The volatility index fell to an intra-day low of 14.93 from its previous close of 14.06. The Nifty 50 fell as much as 1.32 per cent to a low of 22,845, breaching the psychological mark of 22,900. The BSE Sensex cracked 1.52 per cent, or 1,140.76 points, to the day's low of 73,708.54.
In the Nifty 50, Axis Bank was the biggest loser, crashing 5 per cent. It was followed by Infosys, HDFC Bank, Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles (PV), Trent, and many others. However, the PSU Banks held their ground in today's weak session and traded in the green. Except for the Nifty PSU Bank, all the sectoral indices were trading in the red and crashed over 0.5 per cent. The Nifty PSU Bank index was up 2.8 per cent. 
The probable triggers behind the fall could be Foreign Institutional Investor (FII) outflow, rising inflation, and a fall in private banks. 
FIIs have net bought equities worth Rs 18,785.67 crore on Friday (October 16), according to exchange data. However, in October 2026 so far, FIIs were net sellers of $52,100 crore, which is the third-biggest monthly churn out in 2026. Over the last 10 months, Indian primary markets witnessed FII net outflows of Rs 3,12,402 crore. 
Private Bank stocks dropped as much as 5 per cent in today’s trade after their margins felt pressure in the second quarter of the current financial year. HDFC Bank’s Net Interest Margin (NIM) fell 14 basis points (bps) to 3.16 per cent, ICICI Bank’s fell 12 bps to 4.18 per cent, and Axis Bank’s fell 37 bps to 3.36 per cent. Lower margins mean the bank earns less on each rupee it lends. 
The overall private bank index, Nifty Private Bank, fell 2 per cent. Axis Bank was the biggest loser in the index, followed by HDFC Bank, Kotak Mahindra Bank, ICICI Bank, Bandhan Bank, and others.
The headline inflation rate in India rose to 5.54% in September 2026 from 4.83% in the previous month, the highest since October 2024 and ahead of market expectations of 5.4%. It was the 11th straight month of rising inflation in the economy, approaching the Reserve Bank of India's upper tolerance limit of 6% as adverse weather and geopolitical shocks to oil prices lifted the costs of major products in the Indian consumer basket.
Food costs were 5.97% higher year-on-year, with onion prices more than doubling while ginger (62.9%) and garlic (54.6%) also increased sharply. Meanwhile, higher oil prices and a weakening rupee drove transportation inflation to 5.01%.

- TCS deploys TCS BaNCS for Treasury at Indian Bank's Colombo branch, marking its entry into Sri Lanka.
- The platform aims to unify treasury operations across India, GIFT City, and Sri Lanka.
- Key benefits include real-time risk visibility, straight-through processing, and improved regulatory reporting.
- The expansion builds on previous successful deployments within Indian Bank's domestic network.

Tata Consultancy Services has announced an expansion of its partnership with Indian Bank to deploy TCS BaNCS for Treasury at the bank's Colombo branch in Sri Lanka. This deployment marks the first entry of the integrated treasury platform into the Sri Lankan market, aiming to enhance real-time risk visibility and operational efficiency for the bank's overseas operations.
The initiative follows successful implementations of TCS BaNCS for Treasury across Indian Bank's domestic operations in India and at GIFT City in Gujarat. By extending the platform to Sri Lanka, Indian Bank seeks to establish a unified approach to treasury management across geographies, ensuring consistency in deal processing and regulatory compliance.
Operational enhancements and scope
Under this collaboration, TCS will modernize Indian Bank's overseas treasury functions, covering money markets, investment management, and foreign exchange. The transition to a single, integrated platform is designed to support unified deal processing and provide real-time position visibility.
Key operational benefits for the Colombo branch include:
- Strengthened risk controls: Enhanced limit controls and compliance-ready reporting mechanisms.
- Operational efficiency: Reduction in manual intervention through improved straight-through processing.
- Regulatory readiness: A single source of truth to strengthen audit trails and meet local regulatory requirements.
- Strategic insight: Consolidated views of positions, limits, liquidity, and exposures across various instruments and currencies.
Executive commentary
S Viswanathan, CEO of Indian Bank's Sri Lanka Operations, emphasized the need for a platform that supports growth with greater control and transparency. He noted that TCS BaNCS for Treasury has already proven its capability for Indian Bank's India and GIFT City operations, providing a modern foundation for evolving banking requirements.
Venkateshwaran Srinivasan, Global Head of Financial Solutions at TCS, stated that treasury transformation extends beyond automation to enabling speed and confidence in dynamic markets. He highlighted that the solution combines deep treasury functionality with operational resilience, reflecting TCS' commitment to helping financial institutions build future-ready platforms.
Strategic context
This move reinforces the long-standing relationship between TCS and Indian Bank, leveraging existing infrastructure to accelerate time-to-value. The deployment ensures smooth integration with the bank's existing systems and international market infrastructure, facilitating faster deal execution and settlement cycles for the Colombo branch.

articles.summary: Black Monday for European stock markets; Milan (-1.5 per cent) hits its lowest level since May. Tech shares rebound on Wall Street  Il Sole 24 ORE
articles.full_text:
Markets are being weighed down by rising bond yields, street protests across Europe, inflationary pressures and tensions in the Middle East. Bank shares are down on the Milan Stock Exchange. Oil prices are falling but remain at high levels. The spread has returned to 111 points
(Il Sole 24 Ore Radiocor) - European markets, amid rising bond yields, street protests, inflationary pressures and concerns in the Middle East. A period of tension from which the indices are struggling to emerge, with stock markets across the Old Continent all closing in the red and recording falls of over 1 per cent. Against this backdrop, there are also fears of monetary tightening, whilst oil prices are easing but remain at warning levels (Brent crude is above $108). Milan fared the worst, taking a step back by exactly five months, with the FTSE MIB closing down 1.55 per cent at its lowest level since the end of May. The banks’ slump continues, and the sector across the continent has now lost almost 10 per cent in a month. Ahead of the quarterly results, spreads on French OATs and Italian 10-year BTPs are rising, with analysts explaining that “the weekend’s unrest in France and the spread of protests to Italia are not helping market sentiment”. The spotlight is on the start of voting tomorrow in the French National Assembly on the budget bill.
Wall Street ends the day mixed, with the Nasdaq rebounding
Wall Street ends the day mixed. The Dow Jones falls by 0.07 per cent to 51,966.87 points, the Nasdaq rises by 1.11 per cent to 26,430.89 points and the S&P 500 rose by 0.41 per cent to 7,690.79 points.
The Nasdaq has rebounded, driven by a recovery in the technology sector, following last week’s slump in artificial intelligence-related shares. Intel is gaining ground after JPMorgan analysts upgraded the chipmaker’s rating. Coreweave Inc-Cl A — a mainstay of the neo-cloud sector, which lost over 25 per cent last week due to debt concerns — is rebounding. Advanced Micro Devices and Micron Technology are also rising. Concerns about the health of the AI sector have come to the fore after CNBC reported, citing sources, that Anthropic’s third-quarter revenue reached $16.8 billion. This figure, despite representing an increase from the second quarter’s $11.6 billion, has raised concerns amongst investors regarding the pace of growth in AI development. Investors in the corporate bond market have begun to shun CoreWeave, with the company’s credit default swap reaching critical levels. Traders at Goldman Sachs noted that ‘AI credit spreads, and in particular those of hyperscalers, are at their highest levels of the year. The widening of spreads across the sector has forced investors to grapple with the consequences of a slowdown in AI spending growth. It is likely that capital expenditure on AI has peaked, and the debate has shifted to focus on financing, sustainability and return on invested capital, rather than the upcoming earnings review’, they said. A series of quarterly results from leading companies is expected this week, including Meta Platforms and Tesla .
Oil stocks hold up in Milan, whilst banks are weak
On the Pizza Affari programme, heavy selling hit the key players in the Risico sector: Banco Bpm (-3.7%) after Jefferies analysts cut their target price ahead of the results. Unipol (-3.2%) and Bper (-2.2%) were down. Stellantis fell by 3.2%, following the wider European automotive sector. Among the few to hold their ground were Buzzi (+1.3%), as well as Technoprobe (+1.1%), which broke its run of negative sessions, and Eni (+0.7%). -2.2% for Monte dei Paschi following tensions between the MPS Foundation – which is eyeing the OPAS bid from Intesa (-2.2%) – and the local authorities in Siena over the bank’s future.
Oil prices fall, euro above 1.12 dollars
In the currency markets, the euro is losing ground again at $1.1217 (down from $1.1245 at Friday’s close). The single currency is also trading at 177.7 yen (down from 177.6), whilst the dollar/yen cross rate stands at 158.41 (down from 157.90). In this regard, the ongoing protests in France could also affect currencies, according to Kathleen Brooks of XTB: “If these protests were to bolster support for Marine Le Pen, an anti-EU figure, we could see further declines in the single currency,” she warns. On the energy front, gas prices have risen to 88 euros per MWh (+0.6 per cent), whilst oil prices have slowed following the recent rally: December Brent is trading at $108.1 per barrel (-1.5 per cent) and November WTI at $100.6 (-0.8 per cent).

articles.title: European air fares could rise by as much as 20% in 2027, Ryanair boss predicts
articles.summary: Conflict in Middle East is pushing jet fuel costs higher and many carriers are not hedged against such increases, Michael O’Leary saysRyanair’s chief executive has predicted a record increase in European air fares next year, as airlines grapple with fuel bills pushed higher by the Middle East conflict.Many carriers are not hedged against rising jet fuel costs, Michael O’Leary said, which he predicted would lead to airline bankruptcies and takeovers. He forecast these pressures would result in th...
articles.full_text:
Ryanair’s chief executive has predicted a record increase in European air fares next year, as airlines grapple with fuel bills pushed higher by the Middle East conflict.
Many carriers are not hedged against rising jet fuel costs, Michael O’Leary said, which he predicted would lead to airline bankruptcies and takeovers. He forecast these pressures would result in the price of plane tickets rising by as much as 20%.
“You’re going to see air fares rise next year in Europe, I think by 10, 15, maybe 20%. You’re going to see the biggest increase in air fares, I would say, in history in Europe for the next 12 months,” O’Leary told a news conference in Brussels.
Jet fuel prices have soared in recent months, as the war on Iran has choked off fuel supplies. Jet fuel accounts for a large portion of carriers’ costs. The airlines body IATA previously predicted jet fuel prices would be 70% higher across 2026 – estimated to average $152 (£114) a barrel for the year, compared with $90 in 2025 – slashing airlines’ profits.
Ryanair and many other European airlines had hedged their jet fuel requirements for 2026, O’Leary said, adding that Ryanair was 80% hedged at $67 a barrel at the time the Iran conflict began in late February.
However, the boss of Europe’s largest airline said most European carriers, including Ryanair, do not have significant hedging in place from April 2027 onwards to protect them if oil prices remain high.
“We’re 85% unhedged next year, and most of the other European airlines are in a similar position,” O’Leary said.
Ryanair’s hedging contract for 2027 covered 15% of its fuel costs at $85 a barrel, he added, whereas spot rates are currently hovering at about double that level.
EasyJet reported a £105m annual rise in fuel costs in July, adding it had hedged 62% of its fuel requirements for the first half of 2027 and 37% for the second half of the year. The airline announced in October it was cutting 700,000 seats from its winter schedule in an attempt to save fuel.
During his visit to Brussels, O’Leary announced he was cutting 20 of Ryanair’s routes and more than one million seats from Belgium from the airline’s winter schedule, after the federal government’s decision to increase its aviation tax from €2 to €7 in January.
O’Leary is the latest executive to warn of the downbeat outlook for aviation. Industry leaders have said some carriers will struggle to survive the fuel price shock. Passenger surveys have shown travellers are braced for higher fares and are prepared to spend more, but airlines do not know how long consumers will be able to afford pricier tickets.

articles.title: United Airlines CEO faces rightwing backlash after calling for US wealth tax
articles.summary: Scott Kirby says wealth inequality is a ‘danger to society’ and calls for inheritance tax in recent interviewScott Kirby, the CEO of United Airlines, is under scrutiny from conservative politicians and commentators for saying wealth inequality is a “danger to society” and calling for a national wealth and inheritance tax in a recent interview.Talking to the New York Times, Kirby was asked about the growing public distrust of CEOs and whether he felt any responsibility to quell that distrust. Con...
articles.full_text:
Scott Kirby, the CEO of United Airlines, is under scrutiny from conservative politicians and commentators for saying wealth inequality is a “danger to society” and calling for a national wealth and inheritance tax in a recent interview.
Talking to the New York Times, Kirby was asked about the growing public distrust of CEOs and whether he felt any responsibility to quell that distrust.
“We should have a national wealth tax – it won’t work by state because people will just move,” he said. “And I think we should have inheritance taxes that get close to 100% at some level. I would pay them.”
In response, headlines from Fox Business and the New York Post decried that Kirby made $32m in 2025. In response to Kirby’s comments, Glenn Beck, a former Fox News host, and other users on X called for a boycott of United Airlines. Jeff Landry, Louisiana’s governor, said the statement was “audacious”.
“How audacious from a guy that didn’t even build @united and makes $32 million a year,” he wrote on X, adding a link to a government website to donate money to the government. “Better yet, he should distribute his salary to the employees at the bottom of the ladder @united!”
“Let’s see you step up and place your money where your mouth is!” Landry added.
The comment comes just two weeks before voters in California will decide on a so-called “billionaire’s tax”, which would put a 5% tax on the state’s billionaires, that the wealthy have been spending millions fighting against.
Kirby was also asked about the rising cost of flying and said that high prices this year were being compared to the “artificial low” prices from the pandemic, which largely halted travel and highly disrupted the airline industry.
“We have to charge enough that it covers the cost of flying, and it’s expensive to fly airplanes,” he said.
When asked about the $70 passengers must pay to sit in an aisle or window seat if they aren’t a frequent flyer with United, Kirby responded that “the way to give everyone what they want is to charge for the services and products that those customers want,” adding: “There are customers that pay more that get more.”
Kirby also maintained that fares were still lower than in 2019 after adjusting for inflation. According to data from the labor department, the index for airline fares increased by about 20% from September 2019 to September 2026, while overall consumer prices increased by 31%.

articles.title: US judge dismisses sexual abuse lawsuit from Sam Altman’s sister
articles.summary: Ann Altman, the Open AI CEO’s sister, accused her brother of repeatedly sexually abusing her over two decades agoA judge dismissed a lawsuit filed by Sam Altman’s sister against him on Tuesday. Ann Altman accused the OpenAI CEO of repeatedly sexually abusing her more than two decades ago, which he has denied.In dismissing Ann Altman’s ⁠lawsuit, the US district judge Zachary Bluestone wrote that she had refused to appear for an independent medical examination despite warnings ⁠that failure to do ...
articles.full_text:
A judge dismissed a lawsuit filed by Sam Altman’s sister against him on Tuesday. Ann Altman accused the OpenAI CEO of repeatedly sexually abusing her more than two decades ago, which he has denied.
In dismissing Ann Altman’s lawsuit, the US district judge Zachary Bluestone wrote that she had refused to appear for an independent medical examination despite warnings that failure to do so would result in the case’s dismissal.
Laura Politi, a lawyer for Ann Altman, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Santos Perez, a lawyer who previously represented Ann Altman in the case but withdrew this month, said in a statement: “I am no longer authorized to comment on this case but I continue to believe in Annie.”
Ann Altman brought her lawsuit in St Louis, Missouri, federal court in January 2025.
Lawyers for Sam Altman did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Ann Altman accused her brother of sexually abusing and raping her between 1997 and 2006 at their family home in suburban Clayton, Missouri, starting when she was three and he was 12. She said the last acts of sexual abuse and rape occurred when Sam Altman was an adult. He is now 41.
The Altman family has said Ann Altman has mental health challenges and received financial support. Sam Altman has said she began accusing him on social media of sexual abuse after the family rejected her demands for more funds.

articles.title: Frank Elderson: Interview with Die Presse
articles.full_text:
- INTERVIEW
Interview with Die Presse
Interview with Frank Elderson, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB and Vice-Chair of the Supervisory Board of the ECB, conducted by Aloysius Widmann on 14 October 2026
20 October 2026
Almost without exception, banks complain about the high cost of regulation. Do they have a point? Or are these costs essential for the stability of the banking system?
We shouldn’t forget the financial crisis of 2008. The costs were enormous, not only for banks, but also for households, firms, taxpayers and society as a whole. Those costs far outweigh the cost of regulation. The regulatory reforms introduced after the crisis have made European banks far more resilient. Banks today are well capitalised, have high liquidity levels and are more profitable, on average, than for many years.
But wouldn’t it be possible to simplify supervision without putting the stability of the sector at risk?
It’s true that regulation and the supervisory framework have become more complex over time. One of the reasons for this is that the banks themselves differ greatly and operate in an increasingly complex environment. The risks have also become more complex, ranging from geopolitical tensions, cyber risk and climate and nature risks through to artificial intelligence.
But complexity is not an end in itself. We do of course ask ourselves constantly whether we could still achieve our objectives as supervisors with simpler rules and regulations. And we’ve already taken a whole range of measures. We’ve reduced reporting obligations and accelerated processes. But it’s important to remember that simplification is not the same as deregulation. And it is resilience that is the foundation of sustainable growth and competitiveness.
Regulation means costs, and costs can be a competitive disadvantage. What do you see as the biggest obstacles to international competitiveness for European banks?
The biggest obstacle to European competitiveness is fragmentation. Although we have made progress, Europe still doesn’t have a truly single, integrated banking market. Cross-border banking activities remain limited. Banks are not able to fully benefit from economies of scale, greater diversification or more efficient allocation of capital and liquidity across the European economy. This fragmentation leads to higher costs, lower efficiency and fewer opportunities to achieve the kind of scale that is needed to compete internationally. This doesn’t just affect the banking sector but many other sectors besides. We talk about the Single Market, but the reality is the market is not yet truly single.
If fragmentation is the diagnosis, integration is the remedy – not deregulation. We need to complete the Single Market, the savings and investments union, and the banking union, including establishing a European deposit insurance scheme.
Simplification and integration are two sides of the same coin, which is the competitiveness agenda. We need both and we need both at the same time. This is why it is crucial that the European Commission’s banking reform package keeps both sides together.
How much would a fully integrated banking market actually encourage cross-border lending? Local banks know their customers best. And competition is already really strong in countries like Austria.
I haven’t got a crystal ball. What is clear, though, is that a single jurisdiction with several hundred million customers would lead to more competition, better products and more risk sharing. Banks would also be in a position to fund future-oriented investments; the challenges associated with the climate and nature crises, the energy transition and demographics are enormous.
Today, differences in legal frameworks, insolvency regimes and consumer protection rules still make cross-border banking unnecessarily complex and costly. No one is forcing us Europeans to keep these obstacles in the market. We’ve built them ourselves – we can, and should, also remove them and do so urgently. And with the enormous investment challenges in front of us, we’ve no time to lose.
Other countries could relieve the burden on their banks by implementing Basel III more loosely. Wouldn’t this cause Europe to become less competitive?
Banking is a global business. Capital flows across frontiers, banks are interrelated, and risks don’t normally come to a halt at national borders. That’s why international standards are so important. We want banks to compete on how efficient and innovative they are and how well they manage their risks, and not on who operates under the weakest rules. Thanks to the Basel standards, this is what’s happening, because we’ve created a broadly consistent international framework. The Basel standards create a common minimum benchmark for banking regulation and prudential supervision. Of course there is also space for national variations, where these are justified, carefully targeted and supported by evidence. But in a global financial system where shocks can propagate across borders, policymakers share a responsibility to observe minimum standards. Simply lowering the standards does not cause the risks to disappear. Supervisors will still need to assess the risks and ensure banks address them appropriately. Loosening Pillar 1 requirements could therefore simply shift the burden from regulation to supervision.
You’re calling for supervision to be more proportionate, meaning it takes more account of the size and complexity of the institutions that are supervised…
Proportionality is not about weakening supervision. The aim is to tailor the supervision better to the banks, using criteria such as size, complexity and risk profile. This is already embedded in the legal framework. For instance, there is the category of small and non-complex banks that are subject to significantly lighter reporting requirements. They only have to report up to 30% of the data that large banks are required to report.
But there is room to do more on proportionality. And I staunchly support doing just that. Right now, the threshold for whether a bank is considered small and non-complex is €5 billion in total assets. Raising that threshold to €10 billion would enable a further 150 banks or so to come under the simplified regime. Another option would be to lengthen the periods between regulatory reviews, where risk profiles allow. And for stress tests, we could make greater use of data that we already have to hand. All these changes would reduce the workload for smaller and less complex banks.
How far can such simplifications go?
No further than the risk. Proportionality can only go as far as a bank’s risk profile allows, and only as far as it does not impair our ability to safeguard financial stability and ensure banks are safe and sound. There should be no change in the core prudential standards. Banks still need to have sound corporate governance, effective risk management, adequate capital and liquidity and resilience in the face of new risks. Not only would smarter and more proportionate supervision lessen the burden on banks, it would also free up resources for us supervisors to concentrate on the most important risks.
What risks does artificial intelligence raise for banks?
AI has enormous potential for banks. It can improve risk management, facilitate the processing of information, reinforce fraud detection and raise efficiency. But every transformative technology also creates risks.
One area of concern is cyber risk. Advanced AI models can discover and exploit vulnerabilities more quickly. This is why, back in July, we asked the banks to reassess their cybersecurity measures and to review their IT budgets and staffing levels. They are expected to submit concrete action plans for dealing with AI-related cyber risks to us by the end of October.
Banks should not become overly dependent on AI models either. The technology has many advantages – helping to improve credit assessments, for instance. But banks need to watch out for biases and blind spots; they can’t simply leave decisions to the algorithm. A third issue is data quality. AI is only as good as the data it is trained on. And fourthly, operational dependencies on cloud providers, for instance, are emerging. The fact that there only so many such providers is giving rise to considerable concentration risk.
The AI investment boom in the United States is increasingly funded via private credit – loans extended outside of the banking sector – and corporate bonds. It remains to be seen whether the AI firms can actually generate the predicted profits that they use to justify the investment. To what extent does this create risks for European banks?
The key issue here is the interconnectedness between banks and non-banks. We’re taking this topic very seriously and want to see that the banks are also well aware of these risks.
A more diverse financial system is a good thing. Europe needs huge investments to address its strategic priorities, and market-based finance can play a role there alongside banks. Certain other players are better able to bear specific risks than banks. But if lending migrates out of the banking system, it does not automatically mean that all the associated risks migrate with it. Those risks can feed back into the banking system, because of the interconnections between banks and non-banks. It may be the case, for instance, that a bank not only lends money to a private credit provider but at the same time funds firms to which this provider also extends loans. This can give rise to risk concentrations that are not evident at first glance but that come to light when something goes wrong. That is why banks need to take a very close look at these linkages and make sure they can manage them appropriately.
